  • Settled, neuromuscular blocking agents: both incidence and distressing awareness are higher with neuromuscular blockade (Sandin: 0.18% versus 0.1%; NAP5). The authors consider that avoiding or limiting neuromuscular blockers may be the most effective available measure against traumatic awareness.
  • Unsettled, true versus false reports: the Brice questions are not psychometrically validated and may “elicit false reports or memories”. Many report awareness only at later interviews. Distinguishing true from false reports is difficult, and experts often disagree about “possible” awareness. Most dream reports are probably unrelated to awareness and likely occur during emergence (Leslie 2007 and 2009), but Samuelsson 2008 found awareness 19 times more common among patients who reported dreaming, so the relationship is unsettled.
  • Unsettled, IFT as a distinct state: the authors consider that an unequivocal IFT response should be regarded as consciousness until the opposite is shown. Pandit proposes a “third state” (“dysanaesthesia”) in which the patient follows a simple command without a conscious self, but without data.
  • Otherwise unsettled: a genetic component, the psychological consequences of awareness without recall (little evidence that implicit memory causes PTSD), and whether unwanted awareness during sedation is a clinical problem.
  • Relevance for chapter 8 versus figure 36.1: that the Brice interview can produce false reports or false memories, and that an AWR report cannot be verified against an objective measurement, is the closest support in the sources for the sentence “Occasionally AWR may present absent of conscious experience at the time”. Read this way, the sentence is about reports, not about genuine episodic memory being formed without experience, and then it does not conflict with chapter 8. This is an interpretation; neither chapter says so explicitly.
  • Caveats: narrative review without a systematic search. Avidan was on the BJA editorial board. Several of the cited studies are the authors’ own.
Mashour and Avidan. Br J Anaesth 2015;115(suppl 1):i20–i26

Rats without a cortex still move: where in the brainstem is MAC influenced? (Jinks 2010)

Anesthesiology 2010;112:316–324. Adult male rats received isoflurane. MAC was measured with tail clamp and hindlimb EMG before and at least 90 minutes after a single transection of the brainstem at different levels, or after removal of the cerebellum. In addition, the mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR) in the midbrain was inactivated with lidocaine, and its nerve cells were recorded.

  • Starting point: removing everything rostral to the midbrain (the forebrain, including the cortex) changes neither MAC nor the movement pattern (Rampil 1993). Chronic spinal transection, however, reduces MAC by about 50%, and when isoflurane reaches only the spinal cord, MAC falls by more than 30%. The brainstem thus helps keep MAC up by counteracting the depression in the spinal cord.
  • Transections at different levels: intact MAC was 1.3%. After a mid-collicular transection MAC was 90% of the intact value, just caudal to the colliculi (pons) 60%, at the pontomedullary junction 55%, mid-medulla (caudal to the RVM) 91% but with only weak single movements, and at the obex 40%. Without the cerebellum MAC was 95%, which was not significant.
  • MLR inactivated: lidocaine in the MLR on both sides reduced MAC by 32%, and the effect wore off after 20–60 minutes. Injections just above and below the MLR did not affect MAC. At 0.6 MAC, movements became fewer and weaker.
  • MLR neurons: at 1.2 MAC isoflurane, the response to strong tail clamp was reduced to 13% of the number of action potentials without isoflurane. Between 0 and 0.8 MAC only the peak firing rate fell (to 74%).
  • The authors’ model: the MLR promotes movement by driving the locomotor circuits in the ventral horn of the spinal cord, where inhaled agents appear to produce immobility. The rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) inhibits nociceptive transmission, while the dorsal reticular nucleus (MdD) in the caudal medulla facilitates it. MAC thus becomes the sum of direct depression in the spinal cord and these descending influences.
  • Context in the app: the study is about immobility. It says nothing about consciousness, which MAC does not measure (see the Akinesia component).
  • Caveats: rats and isoflurane only. The head was fixed, so head turning was not assessed. Each animal had one transection, and three animals were excluded because the transection did not fit any group. The RVM was not selectively lesioned. Trauma from the transection could in principle affect MAC, but the authors argue it does not explain the findings. Funded by the NIH.
Jinks et al. Anesthesiology 2010;112:316–324

Test yourself: where does this belong?

Tap a scenario to see the classification.

1. Patient receives low-dose propofol, talks coherently, and remembers nothing afterwards.

Conscious, but no recall. Amnesia without unconsciousness. Chapter 8 uses this as an example of the drugs having their own amnestic effects.

2. Patient with neuromuscular blockers and frontal alpha-delta squeezes the hand on command (isolated forearm), but remembers nothing.

Connected consciousness without recall. Alpha-delta does not rule out connected consciousness (Gaskell 2017). IFT responses are rarely followed by explicit recall (Linassi 2018).

3. Paralysed patient experiences the surgery and talks about it afterwards.

Awareness with recall (AWR). Consciousness and explicit recall. This is what we know as the feared complication.

4. Patient dreams during the anaesthetic.

Disconnected consciousness. The experience is not connected to the surroundings. Chapters 8 and 36 use this as an example of disconnected consciousness, and as a state in late emergence. Leslie 2009 (300 patients) found that dreams reported “during the anaesthetic” most likely occur just before emergence, with a REM-like EEG in the last 5 minutes before the interview, and that none of the dreams indicated memory of the operation. See the card on dreaming in the Agents tab.

5. The patient wakes and follows commands before extubation, but does not remember it later.

Conscious, but no recall. Example from chapter 8 of consciousness not leading to recall when anaesthetic agents are present.

6. Deep anaesthesia with burst suppression and no response.

No consciousness. Chapter 36 says that burst suppression ensures unconsciousness, but that it does not ensure absence of movement under propofol. Unconsciousness and immobility are two different components.

The components

The colour indicates the component.

An aside: anaesthesia acts on everything that lives

From Kelz and Mashour (Curr Biol 2019;29:R1199–R1210), a review of what general anaesthesia does to organisms from single-celled animals to primates. Not part of the curriculum, but good stories for a lecture.

  • The word: Oliver Wendell Holmes proposed “anaesthesia” in November 1846, one month after the first public ether demonstration. It is Greek for insensibility: a state in which the organism is no longer receptive to stimuli from the outside world.
  • Claude Bernard in the 1800s: experiments with plants led him to propose that the capacity to be anaesthetised is a definition of life: “that which lives must sense and can be anaesthetised, the rest is dead”.
  • The same dose for everyone: bacteria, yeast, worms, flies, plants and humans undergo functional failure within an approximately tenfold concentration range for volatile anaesthetics. Between the most and least sensitive mouse strains the difference is less than 40%.
  • Plants: ether and lidocaine stop leaf closure in Mimosa pudica, the trap in the Venus flytrap and the tentacles in sundew, and block the action potentials in the Venus flytrap (Yokawa 2018). Plants can moreover emit anaesthetic gases when stressed, perhaps as a self-regulating loop (Yokawa 2019).
  • The firefly enzyme: Meyer and Overton’s correlation between lipid solubility and potency holds over six orders of magnitude. But so does the inhibition of firefly luciferase by anaesthetics in a cell-free system, and mirror-image isomers with equal lipid solubility have different potency. This helped bring down the pure lipid theory.
  • Mitochondria: in the roundworm C. elegans the gas-1 mutation in complex I gives a 25–80% lower effective dose of several ethers. The same applies to mice, and humans with complex I disease are highly sensitive to volatile anaesthetics, whereas those with defects in complexes II–IV are not.
  • Without a brain, without neurons: C. elegans has no brain and the paramecium has not a single neuron, yet the paramecium loses both chemoresponsiveness and motility in a dose-dependent manner. Under isoflurane the fruit fly selectively loses feedback from higher to lower brain centres, as mammals do, and C. elegans develops desynchronised neurons and less information exchange.
  • The authors’ proposed definition: since unconsciousness is only meaningful for a few species, they propose that general anaesthesia is best described as disconnection from the surroundings, both the receiving side (sensing) and the executing side (movement), with a common network principle: lower efficiency and more modularity, so that information is no longer exchanged.
Kelz and Mashour. Curr Biol 2019;29:R1199–R1210

Slow-wave anaesthesia: ddSWA, sdSWA and NSWA (Gruenbaum and García, Lobo and Lamperti ch. 5)

Chapter 5 of Peri-operative Brain Monitoring (Gruenbaum and García, Springer 2025) reproduces four spectral patterns from Chander and colleagues 2014 (PLoS ONE). The terms are used in teaching on EEG during anaesthesia and describe the patterns at the end of maintenance and during emergence.

  • ddSWA (delta-dominant slow-wave anaesthesia): more power in the delta band than in the spindle band. The raw EEG is dominated by slow waves.
  • sdSWA (spindle-dominant slow-wave anaesthesia): more power in the spindle band than in delta. The spectrogram shows a clear band in the alpha range above delta.
  • NSWA (non-slow-wave anaesthesia): low power in both the spindle and the delta band. The raw EEG has very low amplitude.
  • Burst suppression: shown for comparison, with a spectrogram in which burst suppression turns into ddSWA.
  • What the “spindle band” is: the chapter places sleep spindles (traditionally 10–14 Hz) in the alpha range. It also writes that anaesthetics can shift the thalamocortical oscillations outside the classic alpha band (8–12 Hz), and that some therefore use an extended alpha band of 7–17 Hz (García 2021). The chapter does not give the exact boundaries Chander used.
  • Emergence and pain: according to the chapter, Chander found an association between lower postoperative pain and a greater proportion of time in a “REM-like” state during emergence. The chapter also writes that strong frontal alpha followed by a fall in total frontal power during emergence is linked to a lower risk of pain in the PACU.
  • Emergence and delirium: absence of clear frontal alpha during emergence appears to be associated with an increased risk of delirium (Hesse and colleagues, as cited in the chapter), particularly when the patient has received ketamine or nitrous oxide. Burst suppression during maintenance was also associated with delirium in the PACU.
  • Age: older patients more often move into and stay in delta-dominant and suppressed patterns, while younger patients more often reach and keep an alpha-dominant pattern (fig. 5.1). Older patients have less alpha to begin with, so alpha loss as a sign of nociception is harder to interpret in them.
  • Link to the app (the app's own synthesis): ddSWA corresponds roughly to “Slow-delta” and sdSWA roughly to “Alpha–delta” in the raw EEG card above. NSWA has low amplitude in all bands. The transition from sdSWA via NSWA to awake is what the simulator shows as emergence.
  • Caveats: the chapter is an overview, not a systematic review. Chander 2014 is presented here as the chapter describes it, and the original article has not been read in full text. García is a co-author of both the chapter and Chander 2014.
Gruenbaum and García, Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 5 Chander 2014 (as cited)

Why do EEG and the brain's energy use track each other?

Around 60% of the brain's energy use goes to electrophysiological function, which is what the EEG shows. When the EEG is suppressed with barbiturates, isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane, propofol or etomidate, the brain's oxygen consumption (CMRO₂) falls. At burst suppression it is reduced by about 60%. More anaesthetic than is needed for complete suppression gives no further reduction, because the “housekeeping” portion is not affected. Ketamine and nitrous oxide are exceptions, and ketamine can increase CMR. Chapter 21 gives about 50% of baseline at isoelectric EEG with thiopental, whereas chapter 10 gives about 60% at burst suppression.

Miller's ch. 10

Clinical example: spectrogram without a distinct alpha band (“spectral fade”)

Schematic drawing based on a clinical screenshot. The screenshot is not reproduced.

  • What the screenshot showed: BIS 50, SEF 19 Hz, SR 0 and low EMG over about 50 minutes. In the DSA image the power lies in the delta range (red/yellow band below about 4 Hz), whereas theta, alpha and beta have uniformly low power (green-blue) without a distinct, stronger alpha band around 8–12 Hz. The amplitude curve at the bottom is low and stable.
  • Interpretation: “spectral fade” is a clinical term for the higher frequencies, particularly alpha, fading in the spectrogram, so that only the slow activity remains. The index can lie in the recommended range (here 50) even though the characteristic alpha-delta pattern is missing. The pattern is described in older patients (Purdon 2015, BJA; Lobo and Lamperti ch. 3), but age, drug and dose for this example are not given here.
  • Source basis: Purdon, Pavone and colleagues (Br J Anaesth 2015;115:i46–i57) show in figure 3 (propofol) and figure 4 (sevoflurane) that the group spectrogram for older patients (70–90 years) has “a visible absence of power in the alpha frequency band”, and a corresponding absence of alpha coherence, whereas the young (18–38 years) have distinct alpha. The word “fade” itself is not used in the article. Chapter 36 in Miller's uses the phrase “the alpha power fades” about something else: when the sevoflurane concentration rises above about 1.7%, the alpha peak slows to 7–8 Hz and the alpha power fades, so that almost all activity lies in an extended delta band (fig. 36.7). A spectrogram without alpha can thus be due to age, deep anaesthesia or both.
Clinical example, drawn schematically Purdon 2015, BJA

Age and EEG under propofol and sevoflurane: 18–90 years (Purdon 2015, BJA)

  • Design: retrospective observational study at MGH of 155 adults (propofol 60, sevoflurane 95), analysed in a 2-minute window about 10 minutes after the start of surgery with four-channel frontal EEG. Windows with burst suppression, artefacts and transition to emergence were excluded. The young (18–38 years) and older (70–90 years) groups had 18 and 8 patients for propofol and 34 and 12 for sevoflurane. Anaesthesia was not protocol-driven.
  • Power fell with age in all bands: in older patients slow power was 4.9 dB lower (propofol, about 1.8 times smaller amplitude) and 5.5 dB lower (sevoflurane, about 1.9 times). Alpha power was 8.7 dB lower (propofol, about 2.7 times) and 8.6 dB lower (sevoflurane, about 2.7 times). Overall the oscillations were about 2–3 times smaller in older patients.
  • Alpha fell the most: the ratio between alpha and slow power was 2.8 dB lower in older patients under propofol (95% CI −3.0 to −2.6) and 2.1 dB lower under sevoflurane. Alpha coherence was lower, and the peak frequency of alpha coherence was 0.97 Hz lower (propofol, CI −1.48 to −0.66) and 0.49 Hz lower (sevoflurane). The figure legend states that alpha coherence declines from about 65 years. The effect on alpha was more pronounced under propofol than under sevoflurane.
  • Regression: alpha power fell about 0.18 dB per year under propofol and about 0.15 dB under sevoflurane (r² 0.43 and 0.46), and alpha coherence fell about 0.002 and 0.003 per year (r² 0.21 and 0.32). Middle-aged patients lay between young and older.
  • Burst suppression: the probability of an episode increased with age. It approached 1 for the oldest under propofol and about 0.6 under sevoflurane. The episodes were short, at most a few minutes, and were defined as at least three suppression events within one minute.
  • Dose: end-tidal sevoflurane was about 1 age-adjusted MAC in the whole group, with no trend with age. The propofol rate decreased slightly with age. The authors therefore consider that the differences are more likely due to neurophysiology than to a higher effective dose in older patients, but they cannot rule out hidden differences. Opioid was also given during maintenance: remifentanil in 48 of 60 in the propofol group.
  • What it means for indices: the authors propose that commercial indices (not age-adjusted) may give elevated values at concentrations that produce unconsciousness in older patients, because power in the slow, delta and alpha bands is lower. Adjusting the dose to reach a target index may then cause burst suppression. They refer to a clinical study (Besch 2011) that found more burst suppression in older patients within the recommended index range. They propose that unprocessed EEG and the spectrogram can take age into account by adjusting the scale. This is a hypothesis not tested in this study.
  • Explanation: cortical atrophy and a thicker CSF layer may attenuate EEG amplitude in general (equally at all frequencies), but the authors consider that the additional decline in alpha indicates altered function in frontal thalamocortical circuits. This is an argument, not something they have tested.
  • Opioid: the patients received fentanyl at induction (about 160 µg on average) and often more during maintenance, and remifentanil in 48 of 60 in the propofol group. The opioid effect is not analysed. Balanza 2022 found increased frontal theta with increasing fentanyl concentration in awake patients before induction, so opioid is an uncontrolled factor, particularly for theta.
  • Caveats: few older patients in each group (propofol n = 8), short windows without burst suppression, no behavioural measures and no controlled dosing. Patents are licensed to Masimo, and Purdon, Akeju and Brown report royalties or consulting agreements.
Purdon et al. Br J Anaesth 2015;115(Suppl 1):i46–i57

Slow induction: older patients develop alpha and no burst suppression (Obert 2024)

  • Design: retrospective analysis of EEG from two randomised trials at one hospital in Chile (J Clin Anesth 2024;99:111672): 26 patients under 65 years (median 50) and 25 aged 65 years or older (median 75), ASA 1–3, without neurological disease or centrally acting drugs. Propofol was given as a slow infusion (8 mg/kg/h in older patients, 10 in younger) until loss of response (LOR), tested every 30 seconds. At LOR the pump was switched to TCI (Schnider) with the effect-site concentration at LOR as the target, then remifentanil 4.5 ng/ml and rocuronium. Frontal four-channel EEG (SedLine), spectrogram and band power 0.7–30 Hz; the analysis period was from start to LOR (normalised to 100%) and five minutes after LOR, without surgical stimulus.
  • Time and dose: time to LOR about 8 minutes in both groups (480 versus 473 seconds). Older patients needed 1.06 mg/kg propofol versus 1.35 in younger, and effect-site concentration at LOR 2.6 versus 3.15 µg/ml (p < 0.001). PSI at LOR 75 versus 64 (not significant), SEF 20 versus 18 Hz.
  • No burst suppression: none of the 51 patients, in either age group, had burst suppression from the start of induction to five minutes after LOR.
  • Absolute power falls with age, the composition does not: absolute power in all bands was lower in older patients (delta, theta, alpha and beta, all p < 0.05, strongest after LOR). When power was normalised to total power, the spectra were similar in the two groups; the only difference was that older patients developed alpha slightly earlier in induction (55–80% of the time to LOR) and had slightly higher relative theta after LOR (p = 0.043). Older patients thus showed distinct alpha, only with lower amplitude.
  • The authors’ interpretation: burst suppression at induction is probably due to “overshoot” after a bolus, and older, frail brains respond to the excess with burst suppression. Slow, spectrogram-guided induction allows one to find the patient's own dose, use alpha at LOR as a reference going forward, and avoid the excess. They also point out that the Schnider model is based on only nine healthy volunteers over 65 years, and that the Eleveld model gives lower calculated effect-site concentrations than Schnider.
  • Versus Purdon 2015 (BJA): there the probability of burst suppression approached 1 in the oldest under propofol, and alpha fell more than the other bands. Obert finds no burst suppression and preserved relative alpha. The difference is the method of induction (bolus in clinical practice versus slow titration) and the timing (induction and the first minutes versus maintenance during surgery). The authors themselves write that the finding “appears to contradict” the literature on age-related changes in EEG architecture.
  • Caveats: small retrospective study without a power calculation, arbitrary age cut-off (65), propofol only (not examined for sevoflurane induction), only five minutes after LOR without neuromuscular blockers and surgery, one hospital and one population, and no test of whether slow induction actually improves cognitive outcome. The conflict of interest statement in the article reads only “The other authors declare no competing interests”, without any author being named before it.
Obert et al. J Clin Anesth 2024;99:111672

The cards on burst suppression are collected in the tab.

Sevoflurane theta as a dosing target: a hypothesis, and what the evidence actually says

Theta “fills in” between delta and alpha under sevoflurane, and more theta comes with higher concentration (Akeju 2014, Purdon 2015 Part I). An obvious clinical hypothesis is that sevoflurane should be dosed to alpha without theta, and that this may give less delirium. Here it is important to separate hypothesis from evidence.

  • What has been shown: low frontal alpha power during anaesthesia is associated with delirium. Gutiérrez 2019 (30 patients over 60 years, sevoflurane or desflurane 0.8–1.2 age-adjusted MAC, 16 channels, CAM twice daily for 5 days): in the 13 who developed delirium or subsyndromal delirium the usual alpha increase under anaesthesia failed to appear (4.8 to 4.4 dB, versus 3.8 to 9.6 dB in the controls), while delta rose equally in both groups. Relative alpha was 0.09 versus 0.21 (AUC 0.90, cut-off 0.13), the alpha peak was lower (8.1 versus 9.4 Hz), the difference was greatest occipitally, and it persisted at 60, 120, 180 and 240 minutes. The dose (age-adjusted MAC 1.04 versus 0.98) was the same, but only in the risk group was alpha negatively correlated with dose (r = −0.66). Higher preoperative MoCA gave higher alpha (r = 0.49). The authors interpret low alpha as failure of the thalamocortical loop that the anaesthesia “unmasks”, and point out that theta did not separate the groups. Kim 2024 (148 older patients, frontal four-channel EEG): in sevoflurane patients with delirium, power was lower in 7.5–31.5 Hz and alpha coherence and connectivity were reduced; in desflurane patients there was no difference. Fritz 2016: higher end-tidal concentration gave more suppression, and suppression was associated with delirium.
  • What has not been shown in adults: that the theta fill in itself is a risk marker, or that dosing “to alpha without theta” reduces delirium. None of the studies above tested theta as a target, and ENGAGES (Wildes 2019) did not find less delirium with EEG-guided anaesthesia that avoided suppression.
  • The closest evidence is in children: Miyasaka 2025 (RCT, 177 children aged 1–6 years, the card in the Spectrogram tab) titrated sevoflurane to the lowest concentration that maintained alpha + slow-delta, ended at about 0.36 MAC versus 1.0 MAC, and found less emergence delirium (21 versus 35%, marginally significant) and faster emergence. It was not theta they steered by, but the result is the same picture: alpha without fill above and below. In adults the hypothesis remains untested.
  • The mechanistic argument: that sevoflurane acts on more target molecules than GABAA (Purdon 2015 Part I mentions this as a possible explanation for theta), and that “more disconnection requires more to reconnect”, are two different claims. The first is pharmacology; the second is neural inertia (hysteresis), which has been shown for propofol in humans (Huang 2021, Sepúlveda 2026) and in animal experiments (see the card in the Fundamentals tab), but not linked to theta specifically. Hendrickx 2008 found propofol + sevoflurane additive, so “more receptors” does not in itself produce synergy.
  • Practical, with reservations: a distinct alpha band without broad theta fill is a reasonable sign that sevoflurane is not higher than necessary in an adult, and it is consistent with low dose and preserved alpha both being favourable markers. But it is an interpretation, not a documented dosing rule, and in children theta is a normal part of the picture.
  • The meta-analysis (Xu 2025, the card below): across 42 studies, lower alpha power and lower alpha peak frequency were robustly associated with delirium, also adjusted for age, while theta power in most studies did not discriminate. That is the closest one gets to an answer: alpha is the marker, nothing has been shown for theta.
  • Reservations about the sources: Gutiérrez 2019 and Kim 2024 are small observational studies (Gutiérrez: 6.7% full delirium, no benzodiazepines, interrater reliability not assessed, no conflicts of interest).
Gutiérrez 2019, Kim 2024, Fritz 2016, Akeju 2014, Purdon 2015 Part I

Which EEG measures are associated with postoperative delirium? Meta-analysis (Xu 2025)

Systematic review and meta-analysis from Melbourne (BJA 2025;135:1684–1703, PROSPERO CRD42024564983) of non-proprietary EEG measures during anaesthesia and delirium after discharge from the recovery unit. 42 studies, 13,115 patients, mean delirium incidence 18.8%, 49 different EEG measures. Indices (BIS, PSI, entropy, Narcotrend) were excluded as measures, and studies in which anaesthesia was guided by an index were analysed separately, because index guidance changes the dose and thereby the EEG (“drug-titration paradox”).

  • Alpha: lower mean alpha power (−1.43 dB; −1.67 dB in studies without index guidance) and lower alpha peak frequency (−0.73 Hz; −1.03 Hz without index guidance, I² = 0%) in those who developed delirium. In three studies that adjusted for age, the OR was 0.86 per dB of alpha power, so alpha seems to say something beyond age. The authors argue that disproportionately low alpha points to disturbance in alpha-generating thalamocortical circuits, whereas broadband power loss is more easily explained by biophysical age-related changes (thinner cortex, more cerebrospinal fluid).
  • Theta and delta: most studies found no difference in theta or delta power. Lower delta was associated with delirium in the main analysis, but not in studies without index guidance or in non-cardiac surgery, and the authors warn against building mechanistic hypotheses on EEG features that appear only under index-guided anaesthesia. “EEG slowing” (≥ 50% more delta/theta or less alpha/beta, five studies from the same group) was not associated with delirium overall.
  • Burst suppression: occurrence (yes/no) gave OR 2.51 (95% CI 1.65–3.81, I² = 15%), robust in all subanalyses. Duration was 12 minutes longer in those with delirium, but not significant with the conservative method; adjusted for age and duration of surgery OR 1.02 per minute. Suppression ratio (BSR) was not associated, probably because many studies calculated it over the whole procedure and got very low figures. SEF was marginally lower (−0.94 Hz, three studies).
  • What index guidance does: it weakened, but did not remove, the association between alpha, burst suppression and delirium. The authors see this as an opportunity: guidance aiming for higher alpha power and frequency, rather than an index value, could conceivably reduce delirium. This is now being investigated in an ongoing study, and is thus a hypothesis.
  • Mechanism and vulnerability: burst suppression may reflect a vulnerable brain, anaesthesia-induced metabolic failure (cf. Ching 2012) or both; age and low physical activity are associated with burst suppression. Studies should adjust for both age and effect-site concentration, and a “dose-adjusted” alpha (alpha divided by remaining MAC distance) was associated with delirium in one study.
  • Limitations: great heterogeneity in montage, analysis and delirium tools; low threshold (three studies) for meta-analysis; the subanalyses are exploratory; publication bias could not be assessed formally; functional connectivity and “other” measures could not be pooled. No conflicts of interest.
  • Connection in the app: supports Gutiérrez 2019 and Kim 2024 (alpha), Fritz 2016 (suppression) and Manquat 2022 (lower alpha peak frequency as a marker of something wrong), and nuances Hogan 2020 and Jegarl 2026 (vulnerability versus dose). For the sevoflurane theta hypothesis in the card above, the conclusion is that theta has not been shown to be a marker.
Xu, Arnaout, Scott, McGuigan. Br J Anaesth 2025;135:1684–1703

Slow induction in patients over 69 years, with and without dexmedetomidine (Mehler 2024)

  • Design: randomised unblinded pilot study from Osorno (J Clin Monit Comput 2024;38:803–815, NCT05425069): 23 patients over 69 years (median 74.5 and 82 years in the groups), ASA 1–3, non-neurological surgery over 60 minutes. Group 1 (n = 10): propofol 8 mg/kg/h until loss of response, then Schnider TCI with Ce set 15% below the level at loss of response, remifentanil 4.5 ng/ml, propofol adjusted according to visible alpha band and SEF95 of at least 10 Hz. Group 2 (n = 13): dexmedetomidine 0.8 µg/kg/h without bolus for 10 minutes, then propofol TCI 2.0 µg/ml until loss of response, thereafter 0.5 µg/ml adjusted according to SEF above 8 Hz. SedLine, four frontal channels; only relative power analysed because of amplitude problems in the export. MoCA before and one hour after emergence.
  • No burst suppression: in none of the 23, neither at induction, maintenance nor emergence, in a group where the literature reports up to 70% burst suppression with bolus induction.
  • Dose: time from propofol start to loss of response 9 versus 2 minutes; Ce at loss of response 2.65 versus 2.0 µg/ml; maintenance Ce 1.9 versus 0.5 µg/ml. Time from propofol stop to response 13 versus 17 minutes (not significant).
  • EEG: the propofol group showed the classic “railroad track pattern” with delta and alpha, also in the oldest, with a beta activation around 40% of the way through induction. The dexmedetomidine group had more relative delta and less alpha and beta throughout the course; SEF at loss of response 10 versus 20.5 Hz, PSI 83 versus 74 (not significant). The differences persisted until just before emergence.
  • Cognition: no difference in MoCA before and after in either group, no individual patient with a significant fall, all calm and cooperative (SAS 4) at 10, 30 and 60 minutes. The authors therefore ask whether low alpha power is only a risk marker under purely GABAergic regimens, since the dexmedetomidine group had low alpha without worse outcome.
  • Reservations: pilot with 23 patients, not blinded, no power calculation, only immediate postoperative cognition (not delirium after the recovery unit), low educational level and low baseline MoCA values, no haemodynamic data. Kreuzer, Obert and Schneider have patent applications on EEG monitoring; the others declare no conflicts of interest. No funding.
Mehler et al. J Clin Monit Comput 2024;38:803–815

“Frailty” scores from EEG mostly measure age (Ostertag 2025)

  • Background: Touchard 2019 proposed a composite score (BPTIVA: total power, alpha power and propofol Ce at SEF 8–13 Hz) as a marker of a “frail brain”, linked to burst suppression at induction. Ostertag and colleagues (TU Munich and Osorno, Clin Neurophysiol Pract 2025;10:209–217) attempted to reproduce the score in 75 patients aged 18–91 years from the Chilean slow-induction studies (SedLine 63, BIS 12).
  • Findings: the score correlated moderately negatively with age (ρ = −0.44), and so did all its components: propofol Ce at loss of response (−0.45), alpha power (−0.32) and total power (−0.36). Alpha and total power were strongly correlated with each other (0.82), that is, multicollinearity. “Low scorers” were older (median 73.5 versus 59 years), had higher ASA, lower Ce at loss of response (2.35 versus 2.9 µg/ml) and lower SEF.
  • No burst suppression: none of the 75 developed burst suppression during the slow induction, so the endpoint the score was meant to predict did not exist. The authors conclude that the score “probably only detects an older brain”, and that burst suppression with rapid bolus induction may say more about overdosing than about vulnerability.
  • Early signal: the differences in band power between high and low scorers were visible already 5 minutes before loss of response, so the assessment can be made during induction, not after.
  • Reservations: retrospective, the score had to be modified (SEF window 8–20 Hz) to be calculable in 70 of 75, no outcome data. Kreuzer and Schneider have patent applications on EEG features and age, and Kreuzer declares funding from Masimo, Narcotrend, Medtronic and Fresenius Kabi for EEG training and lecture fees.
Ostertag et al. Clin Neurophysiol Pract 2025;10:209–217

The older patient: brain, dose and depth of anaesthesia (Miller's ch. 61)

The chapter “Geriatric Anesthesia” (Mahanna Gabrielli, Schenning and Deiner) is a broad chapter on physiology, preoperative assessment and delirium. What concerns EEG and dosing is collected here.

  • The ageing brain: less white matter in the prefrontal cortex and anterior corpus callosum, reduced synaptic function and connectivity (hippocampus, prefrontal and temporal cortex). Contrary to older textbooks, normal ageing is not associated with substantial neuronal loss in the neocortex or hippocampus (Morrison and Baxter 2012). This fits with EEG amplitude falling with age while the spectral structure may be preserved (Purdon 2015, Obert 2024).
  • Hidden cognitive impairment: mild cognitive impairment in 10–20% over 65 years, and over 20% of patients over 65 presenting for preoperative assessment have undetected cognitive impairment (Culley 2016). Preoperative cognitive impairment is the most consistent risk factor for perioperative neurocognitive disorders, and up to 40% of delirium is thought to be preventable.
  • Dose: MAC and MAC-awake fall by about 6% per decade after age 30 (Mapleson 1996, Nickalls and Mapleson 2003). Propofol above 1.5 mg/kg at induction is associated with severe hypotension (MAP below 55 mmHg), which affects 22% of older patients (Schonberger 2022). Older patients are more sensitive to midazolam and opioids, and take longer to regain consciousness after TIVA with propofol (Linassi 2020).
  • Depth of anaesthesia and delirium, in the chapter's wording: early studies showed less delirium with pEEG-guided anaesthesia, but large multicentre RCTs (ENGAGES, Evered 2021) have not shown this consistently, partly because the doses did not differ enough between the groups. “Despite this equipoise”, severe EEG suppression, including burst suppression, has consistently been associated with delirium (Fritz 2016, 2018). The authors “suggest monitoring depth of anaesthesia with single-channel or processed EEG and avoiding burst suppression with lower induction and maintenance doses”.
  • Drugs and delirium: the AGS advises against benzodiazepines; chronic use and benzodiazepine sedation in intensive care increase the risk, while a single preoperative dose is unresolved (Wang 2021). Dexmedetomidine has conflicting studies, but a meta-analysis found less delirium (Duan 2018). Ketamine as multimodal analgesia does not reduce delirium (Avidan 2017, PODCAST). Gabapentinoids are strongly discouraged. Spinal versus general anaesthesia gave no difference in delirium (REGAIN, RAGA).
  • Blood pressure: the chapter reproduces the POQI consensus (McEvoy 2019): MAP below 60–70 mmHg is associated with myocardial injury, kidney injury and death, and injury is a function of depth and duration. The consensus is not specific to older patients, and it does not mention the brain. See the Perfusion tab for what EEG can show at low pressure.
  • Reservations: the recommendation on pEEG and avoiding burst suppression is given as the authors' suggestion (“we suggest”) despite the RCTs being inconclusive, and the chapter does not discuss whether burst suppression is cause or marker (see Hogan 2020 and Jegarl 2026 in the Burst suppression tab). The chapter does not describe raw EEG or spectrogram in older patients.
Miller's Anesthesia, 10th ed., ch. 61 (Mahanna Gabrielli, Schenning and Deiner)

Can effect-site models explain hysteresis? (Proekt and Kelz 2021)

  • What it is: a modelling study (simulations), not a patient study (Br J Anaesth 2021;126:265–278). The authors want to show that an effect-site model can almost always be chosen so that hysteresis disappears, without that meaning the hysteresis is due only to drug distribution.
  • Background: in mice and fruit flies, induction occurs at a higher concentration in the brain than emergence (Friedman 2010, Joiner 2013, cited by the authors). In humans the findings are contradictory: Warnaby 2017 found hysteresis in the saturation of slow-wave activity, Kuizenga 2018 found limited support, and Colin 2018 showed that a different effect-site model can remove Warnaby's hysteresis.
  • Main point: the effect site is a theoretical space where the concentration cannot be measured. The time constant is moreover often estimated precisely so that hysteresis is minimised. Two models with identical plasma concentration and effect, but different (unmeasurable) effect-site concentrations, cannot be distinguished experimentally. In simulations mimicking a target-controlled infusion study (like Kuizenga), the hysteresis could either be present or disappear depending on which effect-site time constant was assumed.
  • Alternative mechanism: in models where neural activity has two stable states (a simple “double-well” model and a network of two neurons), hysteresis arises at constant concentration, because the system tends to remain in the state it is in, particularly with little noise. Here the hysteresis did not disappear when the true effect-site concentration was used.
  • Proposed test in humans: examine fluctuations in response at constant drug concentration (as in studies in mice and zebrafish where the chance of failing on the next stimulus increases if the previous stimulus was not answered), and possibly measurement of xenon concentration in the brain with imaging. The authors think the xenon measurements probably will not settle the debate on their own.
  • Speculation: the authors suggest that delirium and cognitive impairment after anaesthesia may be due to the brain becoming “locked” in intermediate states on the way back, but stress that neural dynamics must first be demonstrated in humans.
  • What it means: the article shows that finding or not finding hysteresis in humans depends on the assumed effect-site model. It does not show that hysteresis exists in humans. The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
Proekt and Kelz. Br J Anaesth 2021;126:265–278

Saturation of slow-wave activity and neural inertia (Warnaby 2017)

  • Design: advanced secondary analysis of 393 EEG recordings from four studies: 16 healthy volunteers with slow propofol induction and 32-channel EEG, 21 patients given sevoflurane before surgery, 102 patients given desflurane and fentanyl, and 254 patients in routine clinical practice (age 17–90 years). Effect-site concentrations were calculated with population models. For each recording, the dose-response for slow-wave activity (0.5–1.5 Hz, called SWA) was fitted to a sigmoid curve, and “SWAS” (saturation) was defined as the plateau where power no longer increases with increasing dose.
  • Saturation at induction: found in 92% overall (propofol 100% in volunteers, sevoflurane 86%, clinical 91–95%). Failures were due to movement and muscle artefacts or the dose not being high enough. The concentration for saturation was on average 2.7 µg/ml propofol in volunteers with slow infusion, about 0.6–0.7 MAC sevoflurane, and roughly halved (0.9–1.4 µg/ml propofol) when opioid and neuromuscular blocking agents were used. Neuromuscular blockers made no difference. The amount of power at saturation was independent of agent, but fell with age (r about −0.6).
  • Variation: the concentration for saturation varied widely between patients (0.24–0.9 MAC sevoflurane in those who reached it, and 0.03–1.6 MAC at emergence). The authors interpret this as roughly half receiving twice as much anaesthesia as they need, and about 20% not reaching full unconsciousness at 0.7 MAC. This rests on the assumption that saturation means loss of perception (earlier study in 16 volunteers) and is an extrapolation.
  • Hysteresis: in the 16 volunteers there was no consistent difference in the mean concentration for loss and return of response (1.5 versus 1.4 µg/ml), but clear hysteresis in the concentration for saturation. In roughly half, saturation at emergence came at a lower concentration and close to the return of response.
  • Abrupt or gradual emergence: of patients with successful fitting at emergence, about a third had an abrupt transition in which slow activity persisted until just before the response came (26% of all in the largest study and 20% in the other). The authors interpret this as “neural inertia”, defined as a tendency for the central nervous system to resist transitions between conscious and unconscious states. Abrupt emergence was more common with higher age (OR 1.5 per decade), lower power at saturation (OR 0.75 per dB) and desflurane (sevoflurane OR 0.20), with 78% accuracy.
  • Confusion: 15 minutes after emergence, 12 of 65 (18%) were confused after abrupt emergence versus 2 of 110 (under 2%) after gradual emergence (p < 0.001), and CAM-ICU was positive in 17 of 65 versus 14 of 110 (p = 0.02). Pain and wakefulness did not differ. The authors call this preliminary, and the figures rest on one study, and the article does not report adjustment for age, which is linked to both abrupt emergence and confusion.
  • Limitations: secondary analysis, model-derived concentrations, 30% failed fittings at emergence (often because the volatile agent was tapered or because of muscle artefacts), and the volunteer study used different electrodes from the clinical ones. Warnaby, Jbabdi and Tracey are listed as inventors on patent applications on detection of loss of perception.
  • Against Miller's ch. 36: the chapter says that patients need a higher concentration to lose response than the one at which they wake. Warnaby did not find that for behaviour (1.5 versus 1.4 µg/ml) in volunteers, but did for EEG saturation. The study itself writes that this differs from the animal experiment it builds on (Friedman 2010).
Warnaby et al. Anesthesiology 2017;127:645–657

End-tidal versus effect-site sevoflurane at emergence (Johnson 2010)

  • Design: 20 adults for elective surgery (mean 45 years) received midazolam 12.5 µg/kg before surgery, induction with remifentanil and propofol and maintenance with sevoflurane and remifentanil. During emergence, response was assessed with OAA/S every 20 seconds after sevoflurane and remifentanil were switched off. Emergence was defined as two consecutive OAA/S values above 1. The authors tested two models for the probability of unresponsiveness (built on an earlier volunteer study), one with measured end-tidal sevoflurane and one with calculated sevoflurane at the effect site (Lerou model).
  • Result: during anaesthesia the model's probability of unresponsiveness was 99% or more, and no patients responded. At emergence the probability varied from 1 to 97%. Patients woke on average 5.3 minutes after the anaesthesia was ended, 0.9 ± 4.3 minutes after the effect-site model predicted 50% probability of unresponsiveness and 4.1 ± 4.9 minutes after the end-tidal model (p = 0.02). The end-tidal model thus predicted emergence too early. Mean end-tidal sevoflurane at emergence was 0.13 ± 0.13 vol%, calculated effect-site concentration 0.44 ± 0.17 vol%.
  • Pain in recovery: 13 of 20 needed fentanyl in recovery. The end-tidal and effect-site models predicted alike (61% and 59%, p = 0.893), because sevoflurane was by then practically gone and both models become a pure remifentanil model.
  • Reservations: only 20 patients, and the authors write that the model's ability to distinguish awake from asleep in the clinically interesting time window cannot be assessed without much larger studies. The effect-site model assumed constant cardiac output and cerebral blood flow (without changes in PaCO₂ or bleeding), and the volunteer study behind the response model had no endotracheal tube or pain. Midazolam and propofol may have prolonged emergence slightly. Four authors hold shares in and receive salary or fees from Medvis (an equipment manufacturer with an interest in the result), and the study was partly funded by GE Healthcare and NIH (SBIR).
  • Connection with chapter 16: the study supports that end-tidal sevoflurane does not reflect the brain concentration when the concentration changes rapidly, as at emergence. It says nothing about concentrations at loss of response.
Johnson et al. Anesth Analg 2010;111:387–394

Hysteresis and neural inertia

When the concentration changes, for example at induction and emergence, the effect lags behind the plasma concentration. The effect-site model describes the delay (ch. 16). Chapter 36 additionally describes neural inertia: patients need a higher concentration to lose response than the one at which they wake, and the difference cannot be fully explained by pharmacokinetics. Warnaby 2017, by contrast, found no difference in mean propofol concentration for loss and return of response in 16 volunteers, but hysteresis in the concentration for saturation of slow-wave activity (see the card above). There is ongoing debate about how much is due to pharmacokinetics. Older age and dexmedetomidine increase the hysteresis, according to the chapter. For propofol, chapter 21 gives an equilibration time for EEG effect of about 2.5 minutes (time to peak about 90–100 seconds) and about 7 minutes for the haemodynamic depression. Chapter 21 also states that the waking concentration (about 2.2 µg/ml) equals the concentration for loss of response when equilibration is allowed (Kazama 1998). This nuances neural inertia and fits with the debate chapter 36 refers to. Chapter 16 also points out that end-tidal sevoflurane is inaccurate when the vaporiser setting is changed, because it does not account for the delay to the effect site (Johnson 2010; see the card above).

The simulator above does not model hysteresis. Induction and emergence are symmetrical.

Miller's ch. 16, 21 and 36

Artefacts and sources of error in EEG

Chapter 36 stresses that EEG is highly sensitive to noise. Below are the most common patterns and how they appear in raw EEG and spectrogram.

  • Scaling: if μV per division is too large (for example 200 μV), an alpha-delta wave of about 40 μV looks small and can be mistaken for awake EEG or an isoelectric line. If the scale is too small, the same wave looks like noise. The colour scale in the spectrogram should be set higher in the young (larger amplitude) and lower in older patients.
  • Impedance: should be low, usually under 5–8 kΩ, and roughly equal for all electrodes. Clean the skin with an alcohol wipe or adjust the electrodes.
  • Eye blinks and movement: give large deflections frontally. In the spectrogram, blinks appear as thin, vertical red lines. Persistent blinking or head and eye movement can be mistaken for strong delta activity.
  • Electrocautery: gives high-amplitude, high-frequency deflections in raw EEG and a block of high power across all frequencies in the spectrogram.
  • ECG: sharp peaks in time with the heart rate, particularly in patients with a short, thick neck and during burst suppression. In the spectrogram this gives horizontal bands that drift with the heart rate.
  • EMG: increases power broadly across many frequencies, and raw EEG looks “fuzzy”. The chapter says that EMG is not just noise, but a signal that the patient is grimacing and probably needs more anaesthesia or analgesia. EMG is often present at induction and emergence.

The chapter also describes that loss of EMG when neuromuscular blockers are given can lower BIS into the target range in awake volunteers (Schuller 2015). Alpha-delta was nevertheless absent in raw EEG and spectrogram, so the state could be recognised. An example of a false negative is a syringe swap that gives a neuromuscular blocker to an awake patient.

Scenario (table 36.3)Type
Neuromuscular blocker given to an awake patient, EMG disappears and the index lands in the target rangeFalse negative
Connected consciousness (IFT response) with apparently adequate anaesthesia and alpha-delta, without recallFalse negative
Wrong scaling: good alpha-delta interpreted as awake or noiseFalse negative
Burst suppression with noisy baseline interpreted as “awake”, and a deeply anaesthetised patient receives moreFalse positive
Low amplitude in older patients gives a high index and excess anaesthesiaFalse positive
Miller's ch. 36 (Schuller 2015, Hight 2017)

BIS in awake subjects with neuromuscular blockade (Schuller 2015)

  • Design: 11 healthy anaesthetists (29–52 years, ASA I–II, BMI under 25) received suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg in one trial and rocuronium 0.7 mg/kg in another (at least two weeks later). Rocuronium was reversed with sugammadex. An isolated forearm (cuff above systolic pressure) allowed them to respond with hand signals. Two BIS monitors (Vista from 2013 and A2000 from 2003) were used simultaneously, with standard 22-channel EEG. Cognition was tested with mental arithmetic every 2 minutes and a short story to be remembered.
  • Result: BIS fell after the block set in during all trials and did not return to baseline until muscle activity had returned. The pattern was two-stage: first a fall to about 75–85 (median 81 after suxamethonium), and after about 4 minutes a further fall to lower values (median 66 after suxamethonium and 73 after rocuronium). The lowest value was 44 (A2000) and 47 (Vista) after suxamethonium, and 46 after rocuronium. BIS was below 60 in some trials for several minutes, longest 211 seconds (A2000, suxamethonium) and 202 seconds (A2000, rocuronium).
  • The participants were awake: all answered questions, the arithmetic was answered with 96% accuracy and the story was retold with 94% accuracy. Raw EEG looked awake with low amplitude and high frequency, just without EMG and eye movements. “BetaRatio” (a sub-parameter in the algorithm) fell in all.
  • SQI: the signal quality index rose to 90–100 when the block set in, that is, “best” exactly when BIS gave the most misleadingly low values. After sugammadex, first movement came after 27 seconds on average and BIS above 90 after 70 seconds (Vista) and 86 seconds (A2000).
  • Reservations: only ten subjects per drug, and the monitors had electrodes on opposite sides of the forehead and could differ by up to 15 units. The findings apply to BIS and two versions of the algorithm. The study does not show how often this happens in patients. The authors argue that BIS values with and without neuromuscular blockers are not comparable, and that the range 60–75 towards the end of the procedure may be compatible with full consciousness when neuromuscular blockers have been given. No conflicts of interest are declared, and the study was funded by the Cairns Anaesthetists' Association.
Schuller et al. Br J Anaesth 2015;115 suppl 1:i95–i103

EMG activation at emergence (Hight 2017)

  • Design: observational study from one hospital in New Zealand. Frontal EEG and EMG (70–110 Hz, as BIS calculates it) were recorded in 273 adults (16–90 years, 119 with endotracheal tube and 154 with laryngeal mask) during emergence after volatile anaesthesia (sevoflurane 203, desflurane 60, isoflurane 10). The concentration in the brain (CeMAC, without age correction) was calculated from end-tidal gas with a model. Pain was assessed on a 0–10 scale immediately after emergence, and “high pain” was 5 or more.
  • EMG activation: most often came abruptly as an increase of 10–20 dB. In 57% there was one activation, in 37% two and in 6% three. In 11% the activation came already at a surgical level of anaesthesia, and in 15% only when the patient responded to command. In the subsample with detailed observations (184), 56% came after an external stimulus (transfer to another bed 41%, name spoken 17%, airway suction 15%), and only 57% had visible movement. 43% had a hidden increase in muscle tone without visible movement.
  • Two processes: the distribution of CeMAC at first EMG activation had two peaks, divided at 0.07 MAC. “High-MAC” activation occurred independently of emergence, was not linked to severe pain afterwards and occurred while EEG still showed delta and alpha. It was more common with endotracheal tube. “Low-MAC” activation occurred near zero MAC at the same time as the patient woke. Of the 51 with low-MAC activation, 46 (90%) had a laryngeal mask. Patients with a laryngeal mask had about one tenth of the odds of high-MAC activation compared with endotracheal tube.
  • Waking concentration: median CeMAC at emergence was 0.09 (0.07 with sevoflurane and 0.12 with desflurane), far lower than the roughly 0.3 often quoted. Around 20% woke only at CeMAC near zero, which the authors interpret as neural inertia. The cause is unclear, and the explanations involving less aminergic activity and basal ganglia circuits are hypotheses.
  • Pain: the difference between CeMAC at EMG activation and at emergence was the same with high and low pain (0.17 versus 0.19), so pain did not lead to earlier emergence.
  • Clinical: EMG activation on the forehead is often hidden, occurs across a wide span of concentrations and does not mean the patient is waking. It can raise the BIS value. The authors refer to Schuller 2015 on how muscle activity affects BIS.
  • Reservations: observational study with possible hidden confounders. Choice of agent and airway device is linked to type of surgery and age (the endotracheal tube group was older and had longer procedures). Opioid concentrations are calculated from population models. TIVA was not included. No conflicts of interest are declared, and the study is funded by the James S. McDonnell Foundation.
Hight et al. J Clin Monit Comput 2017;31:813–823

Infants and small children under sevoflurane: EEG develops with age

Two observational studies from the same group (Boston Children's Hospital) show that sevoflurane EEG changes markedly through the first years. The children were ASA I–II, without known neurological or cardiovascular disease, and received anaesthesia at the anaesthetist's discretion. 5 minutes from a period of stable end-tidal sevoflurane were analysed.

AgeFindings during maintenance (Cornelissen 2018, 91 children)
0–3 months (n = 17)Slow-delta (0.1–4 Hz). Very little power above 4 Hz. Frontal slow-delta is coherent.
4–6 months (n = 23)Theta and alpha emerge around 4 months, broadly distributed and without coherence.
7–9 months (n = 8)Alpha increases and becomes frontal. Slow-delta is no longer coherent from about 8–9 months.
10–14 months (n = 17)Alpha power levels off (about 6 dB frontally). Frontal alpha becomes coherent, at a very low level and with variation between children.
15 months and older (n = 26)Coherent frontal alpha persists and becomes stronger (until about 20 months). Beta and gamma are negligible at all ages.
  • Older eLife study (Cornelissen 2015, 36 children aged 0–6 months, 30 analysed): at 0–3 months alpha was negligible (peak −6.5 dB at 8 Hz), and at 4–6 months the peak was 6.7 dB at 9 Hz. Frontal alpha dominance over occipital was small and only present at 4–6 months. Frontal coherence (F7–F8) was high (about 0.6) in slow-delta and low otherwise, with no difference between the age groups. Global coherence was weak (under 0.2) in all bands.
  • What changed at emergence (2015): at 4–6 months, theta and alpha power fell when end-tidal sevoflurane dropped below 1.2%, roughly when movement began. No children moved at 1.2% or higher. Median end-tidal sevoflurane at first movement was 0.6% (0–3 months) and 0.4% (4–6 months). At 0–3 months there was no clear relationship between EEG power and concentration. Slow-delta was stable.
  • Dosing: the sevoflurane requirement during maintenance was lower at 0–3 months (median 2.0%) than at 4–6 months (2.6%). The authors also compared at the same end-tidal concentration (1.8%) and found the same age difference, so it is probably not explained by dose alone.
  • Interpretation: the authors link the changes to maturation of thalamocortical and cortico-cortical connections (synaptogenesis, myelination). They conclude that EEG indices developed in adults may give inaccurate estimates in infants, especially in the first three months, and that methods that take age into account are needed. Raw EEG and spectrogram are therefore more informative than a fixed index threshold.
  • Use in the app: the simulator shows only the youngest (under 1 year), and the sevoflurane text has been updated with these findings.
  • Reservations: observational studies without controlled dose titration, only sevoflurane, few children in each age group (especially 7–9 months, n = 8), and no formal assessment of consciousness (movement on video is used as a rough marker in 2015). The authors Purdon and Brown declare patent applications and a licence agreement with Masimo.
  • Awake versus maintenance (2015): in the 4–6 month group (n = 12 with awake recordings) theta and alpha power rose from the awake state to maintenance; in the 0–3 month group (n = 7) there was no change. Slow-delta was unchanged. “Awake” was defined as open eyes, movement or crying.
  • No alpha shift at emergence (2015): in the older infants there was no spatial shift of alpha at any sevoflurane concentration, unlike adults, in whom frontal alpha disappears and posterior alpha returns when consciousness is regained. The study could not assess anteriorisation (frontal shift of alpha), because the dose was not raised and lowered gradually during continuous recording. Two infants in the 0–3 group (107 and 116 days, almost 4 months) had low alpha that fell at emergence, in line with the circuits starting to mature around 4 months.
  • Anaesthetic conditions (2015): all had sevoflurane induction, with nitrous oxide in 29 of 36. Propofol for intubation was used in 19 of 36 according to the methods (table 1 gives 11 of the 30 analysed, see “Discrepancies”). No one received midazolam or other premedication. The analysed period was a median of 77 minutes (IQR 32–93) after propofol or nitrous oxide. End-tidal sevoflurane was adjusted by the anaesthetist’s judgement, not to a fixed concentration.
  • More caveats (2015): movement on video is a crude marker of emergence, and the infants may still have been sedated even though movement had returned. Slow-delta may carry a lot of movement noise. Funding: NIH, Boston Children’s Hospital, Massachusetts General Hospital and a foundation; the funders had no role in the study.
Cornelissen et al. eLife 2015;4:e06513 and Br J Anaesth 2018;120:1274–1286

Epileptiform activity during anaesthesia: can look “deep” on the index and spectrogram

  • Sevoflurane is epileptogenic: in children undergoing mask induction, Schultz 2012 (70 children, 8% sevoflurane for a mean of 73 s before reduction to 4%, midazolam premedication) found epileptiform patterns in 20% without motor signs: delta with spikes (14%), rhythmic polyspikes (14%) and periodic epileptiform discharges (6%). Kreuzer 2014 (100 children) found the patterns in 76% at 8% for 3 min versus 52% at 6% for 5 min; rhythmic polyspikes appeared earlier at 8%. Both recommend a lower concentration and a shorter time at high concentration, and EEG to catch those who react, since it cannot be predicted.
  • The index does not help: Gimson 2021 (scoping review, 8 observational studies, 1 RCT and 15 case reports, almost all with BIS) found that the index value during seizures most often rose, but fell in six studies, and in the randomised trial BIS ranged from 11 to 97 during epileptiform discharges with no difference in mean compared with patients without them. Raw EEG from the BIS monitor caught status epilepticus, but missed periodic discharges in about 75% of cases in one study. Conclusion: processed EEG should not be used to rule out non-convulsive status, but an unexpected index (high or low) relative to the clinical picture should prompt conventional EEG.
  • Two appearances on the spectrogram: (1) “flames”, broadband vertical power peaks that build up and subside over minutes (Taccone 2026, image 14); (2) a low-frequency, apparently deep pattern with low SEF and low index, where only the raw EEG shows that the waves are periodic and have a sharp component (image 19, intensive care patient, confirmed by a neurologist with full EEG). Image 20 shows flames and 3 Hz spike-and-wave from the same setting with PSI 46 versus 23 in image 19: the same type of activity, two index values. The second is the easiest to miss, because everything on the screen looks “deep enough”.
  • What to do when you suspect it: read the raw EEG in all four channels (periodicity, sharpness, symmetry), check the sevoflurane concentration and EtCO2 (hyperventilation and high concentration are described triggers in the literature Kreuzer cites), consider lowering the concentration or switching to propofol, and request a full EEG. Do not steer the dose by the index. Frontal four-channel EEG cannot confirm the diagnosis.
  • What the literature does not say: none of the studies above use SedLine/PSI, and both paediatric studies are from the same centre (Hannover) with the same monitor (Narcotrend) and one visual rater. Adult data are mainly case reports. The clinical significance of subclinical epileptiform patterns during sevoflurane has not been clarified.
Schultz et al. PLoS ONE 2012;7:e40903 · Kreuzer et al. PLoS ONE 2014;9:e89191 · Gimson and Smith, Seizure 2021;91:198–206

Autism: the propofol EEG changes differently with age, and burst suppression is twice as common (Walsh 2018)

  • Design: prospective observation at MGH, four-channel frontal EEG (SedLine) during routine endoscopy, 2014–2016. Primary cohort 42 patients with ASD (DSM-5) and 110 neurotypical, 2–23 years, 120 seconds of stable propofol infusion with no other drugs in the preceding 5 minutes. Secondary cohort 56 vs 123 (2–30 years) for burst suppression. Dosing at clinical discretion; Bayesian regression adjusted for sex, propofol dose, midazolam, fentanyl and epilepsy.
  • Findings: the structure (slow-delta + frontal coherent alpha) was the same, but the evolution with age differed. Slow power (0.1–1 Hz) was higher in ASD at 2.3 years (17.05 vs 14.20 dB) and lower at 10.8 years (16.93 vs 18.99 dB, 80.8% certainty) and 22.5 years; adjusted difference −1.93 dB (80% CI −3.38 to −0.54). Alpha was lower in ASD already at 5.4 years (17.65 vs 18.86 dB) and the decline accelerated to 22.5 years (6.37 vs 11.89 dB, 80.2% certainty); adjusted mean difference −0.47 dB, not significant. Burst suppression occurred in 23.0% vs 12.2% (probability 0.973 of higher incidence), despite lower propofol doses in the ASD group.
  • Interpretation (the authors'): the pattern resembles that of older adults (less alpha, more burst suppression, Purdon 2015) and may reflect abnormal GABAergic inhibitory circuits (fewer PV+ interneurons, accelerated cortical thinning in adolescence) and a higher NKCC1:KCC2 ratio with more intracellular potassium, which in the Ching 2012 model gives a greater propensity for burst suppression. They call it “a form of accelerated neuronal aging”, as a hypothesis.
  • Clinical: an index or spectrogram that looks like an “older brain” in a young patient with autism is not necessarily wrong, and dosing should be titrated to the EEG, not to age. Caveats: observational study without controlled dosing; the ASD group was younger, more male, received more midazolam (mean 0.01 mg/kg, clinically negligible) and had 9.5% epilepsy; in the burst-suppression analysis the ASD patients were older and 21.4% had epilepsy. The abstract gives p < 0.01 for burst suppression, the results section p < 0.05.
Walsh et al. Front Syst Neurosci 2018;12:23

Children 1–17 years: more power, but the same structure as in adults

  • Structure: in patients over 1 year, propofol-induced EEG is qualitatively similar regardless of age, with slow-delta and coherent frontal alpha. Under 1 year, alpha is not coherent (Lee 2017, 97 patients 0–21 years). The same applies to sevoflurane: alpha coherence is absent under 1 year (Akeju 2015, 54 patients 0–28 years; only 4 were under 1 year).
  • Power: total EEG power during sevoflurane increased from infancy to about 6 years and then declined to a level that remained stable from about 21 years (Akeju 2015). The results section in Akeju 2015 gives the peak as 5–8 years, while the abstract gives about 6 years. Reviews and later articles citing Lee 2017 and Akeju 2015 give about 6–8 years. The timing varies somewhat between sources.
  • Higher frequencies: according to Akeju 2015, power in the higher frequency bands (beta and gamma) is higher in children over 1 year than in adults at a surgical level of anaesthesia. The alpha peak and the structure were similar across ages over 1 year.
  • Caveats (Akeju 2015): retrospective study of routine recordings with SedLine (Fp1, Fp2, F7 and F8) in 54 patients, with sevoflurane as the only hypnotic. The groups were divided by visual assessment and had different treatment: end-tidal sevoflurane fell from 3.0 vol% in those under 1 year to 1.9 vol% in 22–28-year-olds (1.3 to 1.0 MAC), and neuromuscular blocking agents were used in none under 1 year and in 9–10 adults. The authors argue that the dose cannot explain an approximately threefold difference in amplitude (about 9–10 dB) in children over 1 year, and that the differing use of neuromuscular blockers may explain some of the difference at high frequency (beta and gamma) but not the power below 24 Hz. They also discuss that skull conductivity changes with age, but conclude that the findings reflect brain development. Three authors (Akeju, Brown and Purdon) have filed a provisional patent application on the use of the EEG measures.
  • Alpha frequency: the sources do not state that the alpha peak is faster in children over 1 year than in adults. In infants, an alpha/beta oscillation is described that appears around 9 months and decreases in peak frequency towards about 1 year, but that applies to infants. In older patients the alpha peak slows (ch. 36). The simulator for children therefore changes power and sevoflurane beta, but not alpha frequency.
  • Practical: the authors suggest that age must be taken into account when interpreting EEG, and that raw EEG and spectrogram are more informative than indices developed in adults. The studies are observational studies of patients who received anaesthesia at the anaesthetist's discretion.
Akeju 2015, Lee 2017

EEG-guided sevoflurane in children 1–6 years: less emergence delirium (Miyasaka 2025, RCT)

Randomised single-centre study from Tokyo (JAMA Pediatr 2025;179:704–712), 177 children aged 1 to under 6 years undergoing procedures with good regional/opioid analgesia. Control: mask induction with 5% sevoflurane and maintenance at 1.0 MAC (2.5%). Intervention: sevoflurane titrated to the lowest concentration that maintained a continuous alpha and slow-delta pattern on the spectrogram, adjusted in 0.1% steps, typically from 2% downwards. All received remifentanil 0.5 µg/kg/min plus a block.

  • Main finding: emergence delirium (PAED ≥ 10) in 21% versus 35% (difference 14%, p = 0.04). Sevoflurane during maintenance 0.9% (about 0.36 MAC) versus 2.5%; exposure 0.8 versus 2.1 MAC-hours. Emergence 21 minutes earlier and 16.5 minutes shorter in the recovery unit.
  • The most important point for EEG interpretation: PSI during surgery averaged 66 in the EEG group versus 42 in the control group, and SEF 24 versus 17 Hz. The index thus said “too light” (above 50) in children who, in the authors' assessment, were deeply unconscious with clear alpha and slow-delta. The authors explain this by the indices being calibrated against conventional practice where 1.0 MAC is regarded as adequate, so that index-guided dosing favours 1.0 MAC. Burst suppression occurred equally often in both groups (22 versus 23%, mostly seconds).
  • What they steered by: not theta, but alpha + slow-delta. At lower concentration the alpha frequency rose and alpha began to dissolve into higher frequencies while delta persisted; this was regarded as the start of a lighter state, and sevoflurane was increased again. In practice this is the same picture as “alpha without theta fill”.
  • The emergence course: all the children passed through a delta-dominated state before emergence. Children who developed delirium had a broader delta band and slightly more beta in the minute before eye opening. The authors suggest that PAED may be more related to the emergence course than to total exposure (cf. Hesse 2019 in adults).
  • The authors' own caveats: the effect on delirium was “marginal” relative to the large dose reduction; with a PAED threshold of 12 instead of 10 the difference was not significant, and an interim analysis means that p = 0.04 does not fully control the error rate (adjusted p = 0.03 with Lan-DeMets, 0.05 with O'Brien-Fleming). One anaesthetist with EEG training delivered all the anaesthetics, at Japan's largest children's hospital, so the result is not readily transferable. Awareness was not investigated with a structured interview; the maintenance concentration was about 1.4 × MAC-awake for the age group.
  • Conflicts of interest: Masimo provided Root, SedLine and paediatric sensors; Miyasaka and Nagasaka report non-financial support from Masimo, Nagasaka is a consultant for Masimo, and Brown receives royalties from Masimo. Masimo saw the manuscript without editorial rights.
  • Context in the app: supports that the indices cannot be used uncritically in children (images 1, 7 and 18 in the image quiz), and is the closest evidence for the hypothesis of dosing sevoflurane to the alpha pattern and no higher (the card on sevoflurane theta). Earlier RCTs with index-guided dosing (Frederick 2016, Long 2022, Han 2022) gave much smaller dose reductions.
Miyasaka et al. JAMA Pediatr 2025;179:704–712

Three case reports with EEG in children (Brandt 2020)

Narrative review with case reports from Purdon's group (Anesth Analg 2020;131:1043–1056). EEG was recorded observationally and not used to guide the anaesthetic.

  • 2 years, propofol for endoscopy and colonoscopy: at 100 µg/kg/min the spectrogram showed beta/gamma oscillations, as in sedated adults, and the child moved at the start of colonoscopy. After a bolus and 250 µg/kg/min the power shifted down to alpha and slow-delta, the same pattern as in unconscious adults, and the child lay still.
  • 9 months, isoflurane and nitrous oxide for ureteroureterostomy: from an unconscious state with slow-delta and a widened alpha/beta band (7–23 Hz), the 7–15 Hz power weakened and beta shifted upwards from minute 204; the child moved at minute 208, while the heart rate only changed at the movement. The EEG thus warned of emergence about 4–5 minutes before clinical signs. Propofol 40 mg and higher isoflurane then gave about 6 minutes of burst suppression with isoelectric periods and a MAP fall of 20 mmHg to 35 mmHg. The authors call this overcorrection.
  • 19 years with severe autism, propofol for sigmoidoscopy: after ketamine and midazolam as premedication, the EEG showed broad beta. Three minutes after starting propofol 350 µg/kg/min, burst suppression occurred with apnoea and SpO₂ 82%, followed by 12 minutes of isoelectric EEG despite reduction to 200 µg/kg/min, with stable haemodynamics and SpO₂ above 99%. The patient did not wake for over 2 hours. Autistic patients have twice the incidence of burst suppression at comparable doses (Walsh 2018), and valproate lowers anaesthetic requirements.
  • The authors' point: the patterns from adults (beta/gamma during sedation, alpha and slow-delta during unconsciousness, “unzipping” at emergence, burst suppression with overdosing) are also seen in children over about 1 year, with higher power. Indices are assumed to give too high values in adequately anaesthetised children, because beta and gamma are elevated, and raw EEG with spectrogram is proposed as an alternative.
  • Caveats: case reports, no control, and Purdon reports patents licensed to Masimo, speaker fees from Masimo and co-founding of PASCALL Systems.
Brandt et al. Anesth Analg 2020;131:1043–1056
This is a schematic model built on EEG signatures described in the literature, not real patient data. It shows qualitative patterns and is not suitable for clinical interpretation. Ketamine and dexmedetomidine are only described in younger adults in the sources, and for midazolam the sources do not describe age differences. Older patients, children and infants are therefore only available for propofol and sevoflurane.

Drugs: consciousness and amnesia

Different agents affect consciousness, recall, pain and movement to different degrees. The numbers below are population averages from the literature, with large individual variation. They are not dosing advice.

Basic concepts: receptors, ion channels and circuits
Miller's ch. 21 and 8 Purdon 2015 Brown, Lydic and Schiff 2010

Each drug below has its own section on the micro level: which receptors the drug binds to, what happens in the nerve cell, and which circuits are affected. Much of this knowledge comes from animal experiments, cell studies and modelling, and the sources describe the mechanisms as probable, not fully mapped.

  • The GABAA receptor: a chloride channel made of five subunits. Chapter 21 states that the receptor is built from 18 or more different subunits, and that the α subunit exists in six variants (α1–α6). Many combinations occur in different parts of the brain. The binding sites lie at the interfaces between subunits, and the combination determines how well, for example, propofol, etomidate or pentobarbital binds.
  • When the channel opens: chloride flows in, the cell membrane is hyperpolarised, and the threshold for the nerve cell to fire rises. This is why the GABA system is called inhibitory (ch. 21).
  • Enhancing or activating: chapter 21 describes that propofol, barbiturates and etomidate at clinical concentrations enhance the action of GABA, so that less GABA is needed. At higher concentrations they can open the channel directly, without GABA. Benzodiazepines are described only as enhancers of the GABA response.
  • Synaptic and tonic inhibition: the hippocampus has many GABAA receptors with the α5 subunit, which is almost absent elsewhere in the cortex. They give sustained (tonic) inhibition of CA1 pyramidal cells and regulate long-term potentiation (LTP) with stimulation in the theta range (ch. 8). This is linked to amnesia, see etomidate and inhaled agents.
  • The NMDA receptor: a glutamate-gated ion channel. Ketamine is a channel blocker and works only when the channel is open (Purdon 2015).
  • α2 adrenoceptors: G-protein-coupled receptors. They inhibit adenylate cyclase and affect calcium and potassium channels (ch. 21).
  • The arousal centres: wakefulness is maintained by nuclei in the brainstem, hypothalamus and basal forebrain: locus coeruleus (noradrenaline), raphe (serotonin), tuberomammillary nucleus (histamine), ventral tegmental area (dopamine), basal forebrain and the laterodorsal and pedunculopontine tegmental nuclei (acetylcholine), and lateral hypothalamus (orexin). The preoptic area of the hypothalamus sends inhibitory GABA and galanin pathways to these centres. Purdon 2015 writes that activation of these pathways is thought to be a key part of how NREM sleep begins (Brown 2010, Purdon 2015).
  • From receptor to EEG: Purdon 2015 builds on the idea that EEG signatures arise because the drugs act on specific receptors in specific circuits. For propofol, thalamus and cortex, which are tightly connected, are described as not switching off when inhibited, but instead oscillating in rhythms such as alpha and beta.
  • Interactions as clues: Hendrickx 2008 uses interactions as hints about the site of action: additivity suggests a shared site, synergy different sites. See the card «Synergy between agents and isoelectric EEG».
Propofol
EEG signature (Purdon 2015) Miller's ch. 21
  • Consciousness: The concentration at which half do not respond to verbal command is given as 2.3–3.5 µg/ml when no other agents are given. In a volunteer study, half were unresponsive at BIS 63 and 95% at BIS 51.
  • Amnesia: 95% had no recall at BIS 77 in the same type of study (Glass 1997). Amnesia thus sets in at a lighter level of hypnosis than loss of response. Chapter 21 states that unstimulated volunteers needed an infusion of at least 2 mg/kg/h for amnesia.
  • Movement: The concentration that prevented movement at incision in half was 16 µg/ml without other agents, and markedly lower with opioid (ch. 21; ch. 36 gives at least 15). Aitkenhead (ch. 3) writes that muscle tone is reduced but movement in response to surgical stimulation may occur, and gives lower figures (see Discrepancies).
  • Awareness at induction: rapid redistribution and metabolism of propofol may increase the risk of awareness during intubation after a non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking agent, or at the start of surgery, unless an inhaled agent or more propofol is given (Aitkenhead ch. 3).
  • EEG: Alpha-delta during maintenance. See the Spectrogram tab.
  • Time course: The half-time for equilibration between blood and EEG effect is about 2.5 minutes, and about 7 minutes for haemodynamic depression. Hypotension may increase some minutes after loss of consciousness.
  • Age: Chapter 21 states that patients aged 80 years or more need about half the dose of 20-year-olds. Chapter 16 states that the dose for 80-year-olds should be reduced by 65% (Schnider 1999). The numbers differ.

The BIS values are from healthy volunteers. Chapter 36 states that individual patients can become conscious at BIS values from 40 to 90.

Micro level: receptors and neurons
