Titrate one agent at a time, slowly in older patients (Obert 2024, Sepúlveda 2020), and look at the raw EEG and SR after each bolus, not only at the index. See image 16 in the image quiz.
Hendrickx 2008, Short & Chui 1991, Minto 2000, Lee 2010, Ching 2012, Guay 2025

Multimodal anaesthesia: lidocaine and magnesium in the EEG

Lidocaine and magnesium are used as adjuvants to spare opioid and hypnotic. The question is whether they have an EEG signature of their own, whether they take part in the synergy between agents, and whether they affect the coupling between brain regions. The literature is thin and deals almost exclusively with dose sparing measured with BIS.

  • Lidocaine, hypnosis and BIS: Hans 2010 (BJA, 40 patients plus two dose–response series, bolus 1.5 mg/kg and 2 mg/kg/h) found that lidocaine reduced BIS-guided propofol requirements only during surgical stimulation; without stimulation neither BIS nor haemodynamics changed. The authors interpret the effect as antinociceptive, not hypnotic. Lidocaine thus does not “lower” the EEG in itself at clinical doses; it dampens the arousal response to surgery.
  • Lidocaine and interaction type: Hendrickx 2008 has a separate section on sodium channel blockers. Lidocaine lowers MAC for halothane, enflurane and isoflurane in animals, usually described as additive, but with a ceiling of about 50% MAC reduction at 12–20 µg/mL in dogs, which by their definition is synergy. Propofol–lidocaine: one animal study, synergy for hypnosis. Thiopental–lidocaine in rats: infra-additive. Lidocaine potentiates midazolam in humans, interaction type unknown. No human isobolograms exist, and the studies stopped below 10 µg/mL because of the risk of seizures.
  • Lidocaine on the spectrogram: the only thing that exists is Firdaus 2026, two craniotomy patients with TIVA and lidocaine 1.5–2 mg/kg/h: one maintained an alpha–delta pattern down to propofol 1.8 µg/mL, the other developed delta dominance with attenuated alpha and intermittent burst suppression. The authors themselves say that no dose–response or causal relationship can be drawn. Remember that lidocaine at high plasma levels is proconvulsant, so the EEG effect is not monotonic.
  • Magnesium and BIS: Walia 2018 (RCT, 120 patients) found that MgSO4 30 mg/kg before induction reduced the propofol requirement for BIS 40–50 (114 ± 15 versus 160 ± 25, unit not given in the abstract) and gave lower BIS than control for the first 40 minutes, less than dexmedetomidine 1 µg/kg. Mg also spared vecuronium. Memiş 2003 (Crit Care, 30 intensive care patients) found that Mg 2 g/h for 6 hours reduced sufentanil requirements without a difference in BIS, and writes that Mg does not produce sedation at serum levels below 8 mmol/L when ventilation is adequate.
  • Why “propofol sparing” is not the same as an EEG effect: magnesium crosses the blood–brain barrier poorly. A reasonable reading (the app's own, not a source) is that the saving in BIS studies is a mixture of reduced nociceptive response, haemodynamics and less muscle activity, since Mg potentiates neuromuscular blockade and thus the EMG contribution to the index. This is a hypothesis and should be labelled as such.
  • Coupling between brain regions: no human studies on lidocaine or magnesium and EEG connectivity during anaesthesia were found. What exists on connectivity concerns propofol and sevoflurane (Fundamentals tab), ketamine (Vlisides 2017, above) and dexmedetomidine.
  • In summary: neither of the two agents has a known EEG signature of its own at clinical doses, as propofol, sevoflurane, ketamine and dexmedetomidine have. The literature supports that they reduce the need for hypnotic, mostly via antinociception, and that the EEG change you see is therefore most often indirect: less arousal response to surgery, or the hypnotic being dosed lower. In the synergy accounting (the card above) they should be counted as opioid-sparing, not as an additional hypnotic. The evidence base is small, without PSI data, and without spectrogram studies of adequate size.
Hans 2010 · Hendrickx 2008 · Firdaus 2026 · Walia 2018 · Memiş 2003

What another textbook says: Morgan and Mikhail 2022 (ch. 8, 9 and 43)

Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 7th edition (Butterworth, Mackey, Wasnick, McGraw Hill 2022). The chapters on volatile agents, intravenous agents and geriatric anaesthesia contain little on EEG, but three things are worth keeping alongside Miller's.

  • MAC-awake (ch. 8): 0.3–0.4 MAC is associated with awakening when the volatile agent is the only thing maintaining the anaesthetic, versus 1.3 MAC to prevent movement in about 95%. It is the distance between “no movement” and “awake” that allows the EEG pattern to look adequate close to emergence (see neural inertia in Hight 2020, Fundamentals tab).
  • MAC and age: ch. 8 gives a 6% fall in MAC per decade “regardless of agent”, ch. 43 gives 4% per decade over 40 years (see discrepancies). Miller's ch. 61 gives 6% per decade after 30 years (Mapleson 1996).
  • Barbiturates and EEG (ch. 9): the EEG goes from low-voltage fast activity at small doses to high-voltage slow activity, burst suppression and electrical silence at large doses, in parallel with the fall in cerebral metabolism (up to 50%). Thiopental doses that maintain burst suppression or a flat line give prolonged emergence, delayed extubation and a need for inotropes. Ketamine “dissociates” sensory impulses from the limbic cortex, and the patient can look awake (eye opening, swallowing) without being so.
  • Older patients (ch. 43): the chapter says that “some have suggested” that BIS monitoring may reduce cognitive impairment, and that the mechanism of perioperative neurocognitive disorder is unclear. This is more weakly worded than Miller's ch. 61, which proposes pEEG to avoid burst suppression.
Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 7th ed. 2022, ch. 8, 9 and 43

Awareness and choice of agent

Chapter 21 cites a Cochrane review (Messina 2016). It found that benzodiazepines reduced awareness compared with thiopental, ketamine and placebo, and that ketamine and etomidate reduced wakefulness compared with thiopental. The chapter points out that the evidence is weak, because of risk of bias, very few events and differing definitions of awareness.

Miller's ch. 21

Intensive care: sedation for days and weeks

Most of what is in the other tabs also applies to the intensive care patient, but three things are different: the sedation lasts for days to weeks, the patients often have encephalopathy, organ failure or brain injury that itself alters the EEG, and the goal is seldom unconsciousness, but calm, safe ventilator treatment and as little drug as possible. This tab collects what the sources say about EEG and processed EEG in the critically ill. Brief notes on perfusion, ICP and EEG in ischaemia are in the Perfusion tab (van Putten and Hofmeijer, Foreman and Claassen, Lenstra, Guay, Nycz).

What the EEG can give you in intensive care: eight situations

Intensive care uses EEG little compared with the operating room. Here are the situations where the sources in the app show that a frontal EEG monitor can change what you do. The details are on the cards further down the tab.

  • 1. Delirium: hypoactive delirium is associated with low neuronal activity and an EEG dominated by slow-delta. As the delirium resolves, power shifts towards higher frequencies (Guay 2025). In Eskioglou 2021, however, general slowing did not distinguish delirious patients from others, whereas burst suppression, rhythmic or periodic patterns and seizures did (see Discrepancies). The EEG can therefore support, but not replace, CAM-ICU.
  • 2. Nonconvulsive seizures: periodic discharges and seizures are common in critical illness. More than 25 discharges per 10 seconds suggests a seizure or status epilepticus, and 11–25 per 10 seconds (or 5–10 sharp ones) belong to the ictal–interictal continuum. Both should prompt a full EEG and a neurologist. A frontal monitor can miss seizures in the temporal and occipital lobes (Guay 2025). In Eskioglou 2021, 7% of delirious patients had seizures or status epilepticus.
  • 3. Neuromuscular blockade: when the patient is paralysed, the EEG is the only way to see the brain. Rasulo 2023 recommends processed EEG as the main method of assessing sedation during neuromuscular blockade. Unexpected beta and gamma during blockade should prompt more sedation. Awareness with recall has been reported in 1.8–7.4% of patients intubated in the emergency department or ICU, versus 0.07–0.9% in the operating room (Guay 2025).
  • 4. Reactivity: that the EEG changes with speech, touch or pain is a prognostic sign in coma (Sutter and Kaplan 2012, Miller's ch. 80). Response to voice and physical stimuli typically gives abrupt beta and gamma on top of slow-delta (Guay 2025). There is no standardised protocol yet (Taccone 2026). See the case with relatives.
  • 5. The drugs in intensive care: propofol gives alpha–delta and burst suppression at high doses, dexmedetomidine a sleep-like pattern with spindles, ketamine beta and gamma, midazolam beta at sedative doses, and inhaled agents propofol-like alpha (Purdon 2015, Brandt 2020, Taccone 2026). See the simulator in the Spectrogram tab and the Drugs tab.
  • 6. Burst suppression as a goal or as a warning: burst suppression should be avoided, except to control raised intracranial pressure, and if it is used therapeutically, Rasulo 2023 recommends a suppression ratio below 5%. Unexpected burst suppression should first prompt questions about oxygen delivery, temperature and glucose, and then a reduction of sedation (Guay 2025). Watson 2008 found burst suppression in 39% of sedated ventilated patients, and it was associated with higher 6-month mortality.
  • 7. Why intensive care lags behind: electrode placement, lack of training, different monitors with different algorithms, cost and lack of validation in prolonged sedation (Rasulo 2023, Taccone 2026). Taccone proposes four levels of interpretation, from a simple alert for nurses to raw EEG for the neurophysiologist, and compares it with echocardiography, which intensivists learned to use without being cardiologists.
  • 8. Clinical examples: unilateral suppression that revealed a clot in an ECMO patient, reactivity during a visit in a comatose patient alpha coma from benzodiazepine poisoning in a child, and a flat EEG from herniation in a patient where burst suppression was the goal, are further down the tab.
Guay 2025 Part 2 Rasulo 2023 Taccone 2026 Eskioglou 2021 Sutter and Kaplan 2012 Watson 2008

Expect a pattern: EEG-guided management of the critically ill (Guay 2025 Part 2)

Part 2 of the review from the Brown group (Anesthesiology 2025;143:1595–1618) gives a framework for frontal EEG in intensive care, built on the comparison with the ECG: periodic discharges resemble extrasystoles, seizures resemble ventricular tachycardia, and signs of too little oxygen to the brain resemble ST changes.

  • Step 1, expect a pattern: based on age, vital signs, disease, sedatives and neurological examination. A healthy 40-year-old on propofol 50 µg/kg/min who opens her eyes to voice is expected to show alpha–delta with bursts of beta and gamma when spoken to. A 78-year-old in septic shock on propofol 20 µg/kg/min who does not respond is expected to show slow-delta, burst suppression or suppression.
  • RASS and EEG: RASS −5 without neurological disease is expected to give alpha–delta, slow-delta or burst suppression. RASS −4 to −1 typically gives abrupt beta and gamma on top of slow-delta when the patient is stimulated. RASS 0 to +1 gives sustained beta and gamma, and RASS +2 to +4 gives a lot of movement and EMG artefact. Natural sleep may also be seen.
  • Step 2, signal quality: low impedance, good gel contact, no leads touching other electrical equipment, and electrodes replaced every 24 hours or as recommended by the manufacturer. The amplitude scale is set as low (sensitive) as possible without clipping the peaks, and the power scale is adapted to what you are looking for. Which scales are available varies between monitors. Clinical experience suggests that a very sensitive scale, for example 1 µV/mm, magnifies the trace so much that ordinary activity can look sharp and epileptiform and the peaks are clipped. Choose the most sensitive scale at which the waves are still shown in full, and change the scale before interpreting anything as epileptiform activity. The raw EEG shows the current state, the spectrogram shows the trend.
  • Step 3, when the pattern does not fit: suspected seizures prompt a full EEG, a neurologist and consideration of antiseizure drugs and more sedation. Unexpected beta and gamma during deep sedation or paralysis prompt more sedation and/or antinociception. Unexpected low activity (shift to lower frequencies, broadband power loss, burst suppression) should first be assessed as an imbalance between oxygen delivery and consumption: hypoxaemia, anaemia and low blood flow, as well as hypothermia, hypoglycaemia and severe hypercapnia. Only then is sedation reduced. If the pattern persists without sedation, primary neurological disease should be investigated.
  • How often: there is no guideline. As with blood pressure and SpO₂, the EEG can be assessed every time you enter the patient's room, more often the more unstable the patient.
  • Case 1: a 39-year-old with respiratory failure in burst suppression on propofol 50 µg/kg/min without signs of oxygen deficit. Reduction to 40 and then 20 µg/kg/min gave alpha–delta. Two days later, burst suppression appeared every time MAP was below 70 mmHg, with right heart failure and rising CVP, and disappeared with adrenaline.
  • Case 2: an elderly patient after mitral valve surgery with falling amplitude (from 30–40 to 10–20 µV) before burst suppression, at a cardiac index of 1.3. After mechanical circulatory support (cardiac index 2.7) the activity returned. The next day, during a sedation hold, she was still unresponsive after 4 hours, and the frontal EEG showed triphasic periodic discharges (10–15 per 10 seconds). A full EEG confirmed nonconvulsive seizures, which were treated, and she woke without deficits.
  • Caveats: a review with cases from a single institution, not an outcome study. Frontal EEG has limited sensitivity for seizures and ischaemia outside the frontal lobe. Brown reports patents, royalties from Masimo and co-founding a company developing control of physiological states during anaesthesia. Brown and Guay hold a joint patent, and Guay has received travel support from Masimo.
Guay et al. Anesthesiology 2025;143:1595–1618

The cards on burst suppression are collected in the tab.

Invasive neuromonitoring in intensive care: ICP, PRx, PbtO2 and microdialysis (Lobo and Lamperti, ch. 12)

The chapter (Pusateri and Robba) deals with the brain-injured patient and supplements the EEG material in the Perfusion tab.

  • ICP: normally 5–15 mmHg when supine. The Brain Trauma Foundation has changed the treatment threshold across four editions (20, 20–25, 20 and most recently 22 mmHg), and the chapter stresses that the optimal threshold is uncertain: below 20 may be harmful for some, above the threshold may be tolerated by others. Indication for invasive measurement in severe TBI (GCS 3–8) with abnormal CT, or normal CT with two of: age over 40, motor posturing, systolic BP below 90.
  • PRx: the correlation coefficient between ICP and MAP over time, as a measure of pressure autoregulation. Negative PRx means good cerebrovascular reserve, around 0 a compensated phase, positive PRx poor reserve. Used to find the patient's optimal CPP (CPPopt) instead of a single common target (BTF recommends 60–70 mmHg).
  • PbtO2: tissue oxygen measured with a probe in white matter; normally 20–35 mmHg, below 20 compromised, below 15 brain hypoxia. Below 20 mmHg is seen in over 70% of TBI patients in the first days even with normal ICP and CPP. Focal measurement, so the placement determines what is measured.
  • Microdialysis: glucose, lactate, pyruvate, glycerol and glutamate from the interstitium. The lactate/pyruvate ratio (normally 15–20) rises with anaerobic metabolism; low glucose, high LPR, high glutamate and glycerol suggest ischaemia or secondary injury.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 12

Neurointensive care: CBF thresholds, CPP, ICP and EEG as prognosis (Miller's ch. 80)

The chapter “Neurocritical Care” (Ko and Engelhard) deals with the brain-injured intensive care patient. What concerns EEG, sedation and perfusion is collected here; the rest (SAH, stroke, neuromuscular disease, brain death) is omitted.

  • Functional CBF thresholds (table 80.5): normal CBF 50 ml/100 g/min, EEG slowing at 20, isoelectric EEG at 15, ischaemic penumbra 6–15, neuronal death below 6. The table has no separate reference in the chapter. This is the background for using EEG as an ischaemia monitor (see van Putten and Hofmeijer and Foreman and Claassen in the Perfusion tab).
  • CPP: MAP minus ICP, with the zero point for MAP at the external auditory meatus (the same reference Kalmar 2010 used). Recommended 60–70 mmHg after TBI; both higher and lower worsen outcome, and CPP above 90 mmHg with fluids and pressors increases the risk of respiratory failure. The chapter points out that measures that lower ICP, such as head elevation and barbiturate coma, also lower MAP and can thereby lower CPP. Individual CPPopt (Aries 2012, Petkus 2020) is mentioned as an alternative to a single common target.
  • ICP: threshold 22 mmHg (BTF 2017, Carney), but the chapter states outright that both indication and threshold are more expert- than evidence-based. The only randomised trial (Chesnut 2012, BEST-TRIP) found no effect of ICP measurement on long-term outcome, while an observational study from 146 ICUs suggested lower 6-month mortality. Time above threshold counts: ICP 20 mmHg for over 37 minutes worsened outcome, shorter episodes did not (Güiza 2015), and impaired autoregulation or CPP below 50 makes the patient less tolerant of high ICP.
  • Autoregulation: PRx (correlation of ICP against arterial pressure, −1 to +1) is the established continuous measure, but TCD velocity, PbtO2 or NIRS can be used instead of ICP to calculate an autoregulation index. Absent autoregulation is more often associated with poor outcome.
  • Oxygenation: SjvO2 normally 55–75%, both below 50 and above 75 are associated with poor outcome, but the method is on its way out. PbtO2 normally 20–45 mmHg, below 15–20 is regarded as ischaemia, below 10 severe ischaemia; treatment guided by ICP, CPP and PbtO2 above 20 was better than ICP and CPP alone (Lin 2015, Spiotta 2010, Nangunoori 2012). NIRS normally 60–75%, but low sensitivity for isolated cerebral hypoperfusion in TBI and SAH, good as a trend monitor during systemic changes (cardiac surgery).
  • Continuous EEG in neurointensive care: in unconscious patients EEG should be used continuously to detect non-convulsive seizures, which are frequent and cause ICP rises and metabolic crisis (Vespa 2007; ESICM consensus, Claassen 2013). Automatic seizure detection has many false positives and negatives and cannot replace an EEG-trained neurologist (Schramm 2017). The chapter mentions that pEEG monitors for depth of anaesthesia use the same frequencies.
  • EEG as prognosis after anoxia: burst suppression, alpha coma and low-voltage delta are called malignant patterns associated with poor outcome, while preserved EEG reactivity favours good outcome. The sentence stands without a reference in the chapter. Bilateral absence of N20 (SSEP after median nerve stimulation) is the most reliable predictor of not waking after anoxic coma (Zandbergen 2006, Sandroni 2020). Note that Forgacs 2020 and Jegarl 2026 (Burst suppression tab) describe burst suppression after cardiac arrest as a pattern that can progress to good consciousness; the chapter uses the term without distinguishing between spontaneous and drug-induced burst suppression.
  • Sedation in TBI: agents with a short context-sensitive half-time (propofol) to allow daily neurological examination, with a warning about propofol infusion syndrome at high doses over several days (Cremer 2001). Barbiturates and benzodiazepines have long half-lives and are less suitable; barbiturate treatment for refractory ICP “under EEG monitoring” appears as item 8 in the checklist (box 80.2), after sedation, CSF drainage and osmotherapy. High-dose propofol, prophylactic hyperventilation (PaCO2 below 30), steroids and therapeutic hypothermia are on the list of measures that are not recommended. Ketamine is no longer regarded as contraindicated in intubated and ventilated TBI patients (Kolenda 1997). Targets: PaO2 80–120 and PaCO2 35–38 mmHg.
  • Status epilepticus: third line is midazolam or propofol infusion, possibly thiopental or pentobarbital; in super-refractory status, volatile anaesthetics and ketamine are mentioned. Continuous EEG is recommended to guide treatment and to detect non-convulsive seizures in comatose patients, and prolonged neuromuscular blockade should be avoided because it masks seizures. See the card on ketamine in refractory status epilepticus in the Agents tab.
  • Multimodal monitoring: ICP, autoregulation, PbtO2, continuous EEG and microdialysis together to individualise treatment; the chapter stresses that clinical neurophysiology only describes current function and cannot predict complications.
Miller's Anesthesia, 10th ed., ch. 80 (Ko and Engelhard)

EEG patterns in coma: same pattern, different prognosis (Sutter and Kaplan 2012)

Review article from Johns Hopkins (Epileptologie 2012;29:201–209), built on Husain's classification. The main point is that almost every coma pattern occurs both in intoxication or sedation (usually reversible) and in hypoxic-ischaemic injury (usually not), and that reactivity to a noxious stimulus discriminates better than the pattern itself.

PatternTypical causesReactivity*Most common outcome
Beta coma (12–16 Hz, frontal)Intoxication or withdrawal (barbiturates, benzodiazepines), severe hyperthyroidism+ / −Favourable
Brainstem lesion−Unfavourable
Alpha coma (8–13 Hz), diffuseIntoxication (barbiturates, benzodiazepines, anaesthetic agents)+Favourable (recovery in up to 90%)
Monomorphic, posteriorBrainstem lesion, locked-in+ / −Unfavourable
DiffuseHypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy(+) / −Unfavourable (mortality over 90%)
Theta coma (4–7 Hz)Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, mild to moderate metabolic encephalopathy, severe systemic infection(+) / −Unfavourable
High-voltage delta coma (1–3 Hz), anterior or focalMetabolic encephalopathy, focal white matter lesion+Favourable
DiffuseSevere metabolic encephalopathy, encephalitis, vasculitis, large white matter lesions, markedly raised ICP(+) / −Unfavourable
Spindle coma (theta/delta with symmetrical spindles up to 14 Hz)TBI, intracerebral haemorrhage, postictal, intoxication+Favourable
Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, severe TBI, large haemorrhage(+) / −Unfavourable
Burst suppression, interruptedIntoxication (sedatives), anaesthetic agents, hypothermia+ / (−)Favourable
UninterruptedHypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, severe intoxication(+) / − (disputed)Unfavourable
Low-voltage delta coma (below 20 µV) with alpha/beta componentsTBI, healthy individuals+Favourable
Without faster componentsHypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, severe TBI(+) / −Unfavourable
Electrocerebral inactivity (below 2 µV)Marked hypothermia, severe intoxication with CNS depressants−Favourable
Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy−Unfavourable

* Reactivity to a noxious stimulus: + preserved, − absent, (+) partial. Translated and abridged from table 2 in the article.

  • Burst suppression: in deeper coma the proportion of bursts decreases and the suppression can become continuous. Hypoxic-ischaemic injury, sedatives, anaesthetic agents and hypothermia are the main causes “that determine the outcome”. It is unresolved whether a burst suppression pattern that is interrupted by stimulation means a better outcome.
  • Reactivity after cardiac arrest (table 1 in the article): Rossetti 2010 and 2012 found 0–7% false positives for poor outcome with absent reactivity during hypothermia; Thenayan 2010 found that 10 of 11 with preserved reactivity regained consciousness. Small, prospective studies.
  • Electrocerebral inactivity: requires below 2 µV with double electrode spacing, core temperature above 34 °C and at least 30 minutes, without response to intense stimulation. Hypothermia must be excluded because it can cause reversible inactivity.
  • Historical: the article refers to Stockard and Bickford (1975), who described progressive EEG slowing with increasing depth of anaesthesia (figure 1), the same continuum as in the Spectrogram tab.
  • Caveats: narrative review without a systematic search, many of the sources are case reports from the 1980s, and the table gives “most common outcome”, not predictive values. Reactivity was not standardised (see Taccone 2026). The article is from 2012, before the ACNS 2021 terminology and before Forgacs 2020 on burst suppression with theta in the bursts. No relevant conflicts of interest declared.
Sutter and Kaplan. Epileptologie 2012;29:201–209

Sedation is not sleep

Propofol and midazolam do not produce physiological sleep: sleep deprivation as part of ICU delirium

  • The claim: Brown, Lydic and Schiff (NEJM 2010) write that general anaesthesia “is, in fact, a reversible drug-induced coma”, and that anaesthesiologists call it “sleep” to avoid disquieting patients, but unfortunately also in technical descriptions. At surgical depth anaesthesia can functionally approximate brain-stem death (unconscious, depressed brain-stem reflexes, no response to nociception, no respiratory drive), and emergence follows the same steps as recovery from coma (table 1 in the article). Sleep is actively generated by nuclei in the hypothalamus, brain stem and basal forebrain, cycles between NREM and REM every 90–120 minutes, and serves cardiovascular, immune and cognitive function. Brown has said the same publicly: patients are told they will “go to sleep”, but that is not the state they are in, and he has used the Michael Jackson case as an example (NPR interview 2011).
  • How the EEG separates sleep from anaesthesia (Akeju and Brown 2017): (1) Slow waves occur in both, but in sleep they are synchronous with brief pauses in cortical firing, under propofol asynchronous with prolonged pauses, and with more cortical sources. (2) Alpha is not a feature of NREM sleep; GABAergic alpha is frontal, high-amplitude and coherent, lies in the same frequency range as sleep spindles (12–16 Hz), but lacks the spindles' transient envelope and refractory period of several seconds, and occurs only together with slow waves. (3) Burst suppression and isoelectric EEG never occur in normal sleep; they belong to anoxic brain injury, hypothermia and Ohtahara syndrome. (4) Gamma in REM is not the same as ketamine's narrow-band 30–45 Hz “gamma burst”. (5) Sedation with GABAergic agents produces beta activity, whereas NREM sleep reduces beta; the common sleep medications (zolpidem, benzodiazepines) produce the same beta and similar cognitive side effects. (6) Dexmedetomidine produces spindles and slow waves resembling N2, but K-complexes have not been described. Their conclusion: neither anaesthetics nor sleep medications produce physiological sleep, they are unlikely to compensate for sleep need, and the oscillations they produce probably contribute to drug-induced brain dysfunction. The authors declare no competing interests.
  • ICU delirium and paradoxical excitation: Brown 2010 proposes that delirium with benzodiazepine sedation in the ICU may share a circuit mechanism with the paradoxical excitation seen at low doses of nearly every anaesthetic (GABA-mediated disinhibition in striatothalamic pathways), in line with zolpidem “waking” some patients in a minimally conscious state. This is a hypothesis in the article, not a finding.
  • What sedatives do to sleep architecture (Telias and Wilcox 2019, review): propofol is a potent suppressor of slow-wave sleep (SWS) and produces burst suppression at high doses; benzodiazepines shorten sleep latency but reduce both SWS and REM; opioids suppress SWS and REM dose-dependently. In 21 ventilated patients on continuous intravenous sedation, Gehlbach 2012 found pronounced temporal disorganisation of circadian rhythm and sleep–wake regulation, with few normal sleep EEG findings. Sedation frequently produces “atypical” EEG patterns not seen in normal sleep.
  • Sleep loss and delirium: sleep deprivation is regarded as a potentially modifiable risk factor for delirium, but the direction is unclear: delirium also disturbs sleep, and they may share pathophysiology. Trompeo 2011 found that severe REM reduction (below 6% of total sleep time) was associated with delirium in ICU patients, without causation being shown. Dexmedetomidine resembles natural sleep more than the GABA agonists do (spindles and slow waves, see the Agents tab); small pilot studies showed better sleep efficiency, and low-dose nocturnal dexmedetomidine reduced delirium without improving self-reported sleep quality.
  • What EEG can contribute: a sedation EEG with alpha-delta or burst suppression is not sleep, even if the patient lies still with eyes closed. It is an argument for measuring rather than assuming: the spectrogram shows whether the patient is in a drug-induced state or in sleep with spindles and cyclic alternation. Drouot scoring of “pathological wakefulness” and “atypical sleep” is validated only in non-sedated patients.
  • The Michael Jackson case, what is documented: Jackson received propofol at home for insomnia and died in 2009; his physician Conrad Murray was convicted of involuntary manslaughter in 2011. Expert witnesses at the trial included the anaesthesiologists Steven Shafer (for the prosecution) and Paul White (for the defence) and the sleep specialist Nader Kamangar, who testified that propofol has no medical benefit for insomnia. Emery Brown was not a witness in the case but has used it in public communication. Whether chronic propofol “sleep” made Jackson sleep-deprived is a hypothesis raised publicly, not a forensic finding.
  • Terminology: the sources in this app use “unconsciousness”, “hypnosis” and “sedation”, not “sleep”. Telling patients and relatives that they will “sleep” is established practice, but it is worth knowing that it is wrong, and that “sedation for days” does not meet the need for sleep.
Brown, Lydic and Schiff. N Engl J Med 2010;363:2638–2650 · Akeju and Brown. Curr Opin Neurobiol 2017;44:178–185 · Telias and Wilcox. Crit Care 2019;23:82 · Gehlbach 2012 and Trompeo 2011 (cited by Telias) · NPR Fresh Air 2011 · Medscape and CNN, trial 2011

What the textbook chapter on sleep medicine adds (Miller's ch. 9, Eikermann, Fassbender and Azimaraghi)

  • Sleep onset is sharp, induction is gradual: physiological sleep begins as a sharp alpha–theta transition in the EEG, without intermediate stages, and the same applies to the NREM→REM switch (pontine “flip-flop” switches). Anaesthetic induction, by contrast, is a continuous decline from awake through reduced responsiveness to unresponsive. Sleep has spontaneous onset and termination, is readily reversed by noxious stimuli and is homeostatically regulated; anaesthesia lacks the stage structure, and arousal from drug-induced unconsciousness requires some drug elimination. The chapter states that EEG patterns during sleep and anaesthesia differ despite similarities between slow-wave sleep and anaesthesia, citing Brown 2010.
  • The stages as the chapter defines them: N1 is the alpha→theta transition, N2 has spindles and K-complexes, N3 is slow-wave sleep (delta), REM is low-amplitude mixed activity with atonia and eye movements. Benzodiazepines, opioids and antidepressants suppress REM; the elderly have less slow-wave sleep. Polysomnography (EEG, EOG, chin EMG) is the only method that determines sleep stage precisely; actigraphy and questionnaires do not.
  • The “shared circuit” hypothesis, and why it does not hold for anaesthesia: many sedatives (dexmedetomidine, ethanol, isoflurane) activate sleep-promoting VLPO neurons, and loss of VLPO neurons attenuates the sedative response to dexmedetomidine, suggesting a causal role for sedation. But animals with complete VLPO lesions can still be anaesthetised (transient resistance to volatile agents, later increased sensitivity owing to increased homeostatic sleep drive), and direct inhibition of the TMN produces sedation, not anaesthesia. The chapter's conclusion (fig. 9.12): anaesthetics activate VLPO/MnPO and induce arousable unconsciousness (sedation) at low doses, but general anaesthesia cannot be achieved via arousal-inhibiting circuits alone; at anaesthetic doses, circuits downstream (including the neocortex) are modulated simultaneously so that the brain's information processing is disrupted across spatial and temporal scales. Thalamocortical networks remain active during sleep, unlike during anaesthesia.
  • Postoperative sleep: REM falls substantially on the first night after surgery and anaesthesia, with REM rebound (more and more intense REM) on nights 2–4; disturbances can last up to 6 months depending on the extent of surgery. Surgery alone (without general anaesthesia) reduces REM; pain, inflammation, immobility and anxiety contribute. In long-term ventilated patients propofol sedation abolishes REM and diminishes sleep quality (Kondili 2012), whereas low-dose propofol permits REM. Ketamine is little studied, probably with mild REM effects. Circadian effects of anaesthetics are unresolved; 3 hours of anaesthesia did not alter the body-temperature rhythm in humans.
  • Sleep in the ICU: sleep fragmentation occurs consistently during sedation and mechanical ventilation; deep NREM, REM and circadian rhythms are severely reduced or abolished, and about half of sleep occurs during the daytime. In up to 70% of sedated or ventilated patients the EEG is “atypical” and does not fit standard criteria for sleep and wakefulness; alternative ICU scoring systems (Watson 2013) have been proposed but not validated. Frontal portable EEG monitors with electrode placements approximating the AASM recommendation can be used. Sound above 77 dB increased arousals in stable ventilated patients (Elbaz 2017), with alarms the largest source; dim light around the clock hinders photoentrainment. Earplugs and eye masks consistently improve sleep quality.
  • Sedation depth, REM and delirium: prolonged deep sedation (RASS ≤ −3) is associated with longer ICU and hospital stays and delirium; GABA agonists (propofol, benzodiazepines) may increase sedation depth, reduce REM and thereby increase neurocognitive disorders (Azimaraghi 2022, retrospective cohort from the same author group). Opioids reduce REM and worsen sleep apnoea; unrecognised pain leads to excessive sedative use. Melatonin has produced conflicting results; the orexin antagonist suvorexant is promising but not studied in the critically ill. Sleep deprivation impairs immune function, glucose tolerance, produces a catabolic stress response, respiratory muscle fatigue, impaired attention and working memory and increased vulnerability to delirium, but sleep-promoting agents can themselves increase delirium risk.
  • Narcolepsy: these patients have increased sensitivity to anaesthetics with delayed emergence, postoperative hypersomnia and apnoeic episodes; the chapter recommends monitoring of anaesthetic depth in this group, without specifying the method.
  • Caveats: the chapter is a textbook review; many of the mechanistic findings are animal studies (VLPO lesions in rats and mice), and the 70% atypical-EEG figure comes from a single study. Conflicts of interest are not stated in the chapter text available to us.
Miller's Anesthesia, 10th ed., ch. 9 (Eikermann, Fassbender and Azimaraghi) · the chapter's references: Brown 2010, Akeju and Brown 2017, Moore 2012, Kondili 2012, Watson 2013, Elbaz 2017, Azimaraghi 2022

PADIS 2018: what the guideline says about sedation depth and EEG monitoring (Devlin 2018)

The Society of Critical Care Medicine guideline for pain, agitation/sedation, delirium, immobility and sleep in adult intensive care patients (Crit Care Med 2018;46:e825–e873). GRADE methodology, with patient representatives on the panel.

  • Light sedation: recommends light rather than deep sedation in ventilated patients (conditional recommendation, low quality). Light sedation was defined as RASS −2 to +1 in the studies. Eight RCTs: shorter time to extubation (−0.77 days) and fewer tracheostomies (RR 0.57), but no difference in 90-day mortality (RR 1.01), delirium (RR 0.96), PTSD or self-extubation. The panel considers the old definition (RASS ≥ −2 with eye opening for 10 minutes) probably deeper than necessary.
  • Daily sedation interruption or nurse-driven protocol: both can achieve and maintain light sedation (ungraded). A brief sedation interruption should not be used as an excuse for deep sedation for the rest of the day.
  • Choice of agent: propofol or dexmedetomidine rather than benzodiazepines (conditional, low quality). Dexmedetomidine should not be used when deep sedation (with or without neuromuscular blockade) is required. Dexmedetomidine is suggested in delirium where agitation prevents weaning.
  • Objective sedation monitoring (ungraded): BIS “appears best suited for titration during deep sedation or neuromuscular blockade”, and can improve titration when a sedation scale cannot be used. 32 intensive care studies of BIS against scales were reviewed. Three studies of BIS-guided sedation showed lower sedative use and faster awakening, fewer procedure-related events, and lower midazolam and fentanyl doses, less agitation, fewer tracheostomies and shorter length of stay.
  • Why scale and EEG do not track each other: the scales bottom out at RASS −5, while the EEG can continue down to an isoelectric line; during agitation BIS tops out at 100 while the scales continue upwards. The scales also require stimulation, which in itself raises the index, so the timing of the EEG reading relative to the stimulation determines the agreement. Studies that did not account for this had the poorest agreement.
  • Sleep: advises against routine physiological sleep monitoring (actigraphy, BIS, EEG, polysomnography) clinically (conditional, very low quality).
  • Caveats: most of the recommendations are conditional with low quality of evidence. Several panel members report conflicts of interest, including an EEG-based delirium monitor under development.
Devlin et al. Crit Care Med 2018;46:e825–e873

EEG in ventilated patients with new-onset altered consciousness and delirium (Eskioglou 2021)

Pre-planned analysis from the CERTA study (Acta Neurol Scand 2021;144:296–302): 91 non-neurological intensive care patients in Lausanne (median 66 years, sepsis most common) who had an EEG because of new-onset altered consciousness, median 5 days after admission. 64% were sedated during the EEG (propofol and/or midazolam). The EEG was interpreted according to the 2012 ACNS nomenclature, blinded to delirium. 42 (46%) developed delirium, half diagnosed with CAM-ICU and the rest from the chart and antipsychotic use.

  • Burst suppression only in the delirious: 10% versus 0% (p = 0.02). Of the four, two were unsedated and two received propofol 2.2–2.5 mg/kg/h; all had sepsis, two died.
  • Rhythmic or periodic patterns (the ictal-interictal continuum) in 43% versus 22% (p = 0.03), and seizures or status epilepticus in 7% versus 0% (p = 0.05).
  • At least one of the three findings in 32 of 91 (35%) gave a higher delirium rate (42 versus 15%, p = 0.006).
  • What did not discriminate: dominant frequency (theta in about 70% in both groups), amplitude, reactivity, triphasic waves (33 versus 27%), NREM sleep elements and sedative doses during the first 5 days. General EEG slowing, which is often linked to delirium, therefore did not discriminate here, because it is common in intensive care patients regardless of cause.
  • ACNS definitions used: continuous (suppression below 10%), discontinuous (10–49%), burst suppression (≥ 50%) and suppressed (below 10 µV).
  • Caveats: small sample, selected population without acute brain injury, EEG mostly recorded while delirium was already present (81 of 91), CAM-ICU missing in half, borderline significance for seizures, no correction for multiple comparisons. Funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation.
Eskioglou et al. Acta Neurol Scand 2021;144:296–302

Consensus on processed EEG during sedation of the critically ill (Rasulo 2023)

International expert panel (Neurocrit Care 2023;38:296–311), 21 clinicians in neurointensive care and neuroanaesthesia, Delphi method without a systematic literature review. 59 statements: 47 rated appropriate with strong consensus, 2 inappropriate, 3 with weak consensus, 2 uncertain and 5 without consensus. The document is to be revised after 5 years.

  • Technique: pEEG is suitable for monitoring sedation level; four to five channels are sufficient, a frontal montage is sufficient, and the monitor should display raw EEG with adjustable speed and amplitude scale as well as a continuous colour spectrogram with adjustable power scale (all strong consensus). Whether two channels are enough reached no consensus.
  • The index number: the panel could not recommend dimensionless indices (BIS, PSI, entropy) as sufficient for monitoring sedation depth in the critically ill (uncertain, but with strong consensus about the uncertainty). If they are used, the manufacturer's target range should be followed, and the number should be checked against the raw EEG rhythm.
  • Burst suppression: should be avoided in all situations except to control raised intracranial pressure (strong consensus). Suppression ratio (SR) is a good measure, and if burst suppression is used therapeutically, SR should be kept below 5% (strong consensus). The background notes that age and comorbidity lower the amplitude and weaken alpha, which increases the propensity for burst suppression.
  • Who: all sedated patients where clinical assessment is not possible, all who need deep sedation (RASS ≤ −3), patients on ECMO, patients receiving brief deep sedation for procedures, and separate criteria for older patients (all strong consensus). After cardiac arrest, continuous EEG is recommended during cooling and rewarming or in the event of seizures. During neuromuscular blockade, pEEG should be the main method for sedation assessment (strong consensus).
  • Who not: patients with only light sedation (RASS 0 to −2) do not benefit from it. RASS and SAS remain the most valid tools, and pEEG should supplement, not replace, the scales. In non-comatose, non-paralysed patients the panel could not recommend indices as the main method. Start as early as possible and measure continuously.
  • Interpretation: pEEG values vary between patients at the same clinical sedation level, and are affected by blood flow, hypothermia, age and brain injury. During light sedation, EMG can artificially raise the values.
  • Training: structured training with certification, in the frequency, time and power domains, rapid recognition of typical patterns, and access to a neurointensivist or neurophysiologist when needed (strong consensus).
  • Barriers and caveats: the panel itself mentions lack of knowledge, lack of validation in prolonged sedation, lack of standardisation between monitors with different algorithms, and cost. No systematic literature review, and the panel selection may have introduced bias: nine of the authors report speaker fees or positions with Masimo, Medtronic, Edwards or Nihon Kohden, and one is a medical director at Masimo.
Rasulo et al. Neurocrit Care 2023;38:296–311

EEG as a bedside monitor in intensive care: the intensivist's perspective (Taccone 2026)

Perspective article in Critical Care 2026;30:195 (Taccone, Ozkaya, Baggiani, Rasulo). No original data; an argument for how EEG can become a genuine bedside monitoring tool in intensive care.

  • The problem: EEG is non-invasive, cheap and meaningful, but does not meet the requirements of a bedside monitor (immediately available, continuously interpretable, directly actionable). Electrode placement requires technicians, continuous EEG cannot be offered to everyone, visual interpretation of raw EEG by experts remains the reference standard, and even experts have only moderate agreement on patterns on the ictal-interictal continuum (Jing 2023). For many intensive care teams the EEG machine is “a foreign body” at the bedside.
  • Four things the intensivist needs: background activity (continuous, discontinuous or suppressed), asymmetry, burst suppression (spontaneous or drug-induced) and ictal or highly epileptiform activity (ACNS 2021 terminology). Brief, structured training improves classification by intensivists and nurses (Citerio, Taran). The parallel is echocardiography and lung ultrasound, which intensivists use without being cardiologists.
  • Montage according to the question: continuous EEG is superior for seizure detection and DCI after SAH, whereas brief intermittent recordings may suffice for prognosis after cardiac arrest. A full 10–20 is needed for localisation, whereas simplified montages may be adequate to detect burst suppression from oversedation or highly malignant patterns after hypoxia. Continuous and intermittent EEG are not interchangeable even though outcome studies have not shown a difference.
  • Four levels of interpretation: (1) a binary “red” alarm signal on the patient monitor for nurses without EEG training, for example a brain icon indicating the side; (2) type of abnormality for doctors without formal EEG training; (3) quantitative trends (spectrogram, SEF, amplitude trend, alpha/delta ratio, burst suppression ratio, seizure probability) for EEG-trained intensive care clinicians; (4) raw EEG with montages and filters for the neurophysiologist. No treatment decision should be made by untrained staff on the basis of the alarm alone.
  • Spectrogram and SEF: the spectrogram is suited to seeing progressive background slowing (oversedation or raised ICP) and burst suppression (black bars). Low SEF means deeper suppression, whereas apparently increased high-frequency power may be EMG. Seizures appear as focal “hot spots” that build up and fade gradually, in contrast to artefacts, which are abrupt and do not evolve.
  • Drug signatures: the article reproduces Purdon 2015: propofol gives increasing delta and alpha and burst suppression at high doses, dexmedetomidine a sleep-like delta pattern, ketamine an activated picture with high beta and low gamma, and volatile agents propofol-like alpha at low concentrations, “but higher doses add theta activity and a broader spectral distribution”. This agrees with the theta fill-in in the simulator in the Spectrogram tab.
  • EEG reactivity: has shown diagnostic and prognostic value, but reproducibility varies and there is no standardised stimulation protocol, so for now it belongs at the expert level.
  • Caveats: a perspective without data, with proposals (alarm levels, AI detection) that have not been validated in multicentre studies; alarm fatigue and costs are unresolved. Taccone is a scientific adviser for Neuroptics and Nihon Kohden, and Rasulo reports speaker fees from Masimo. No funding.
Taccone et al. Crit Care 2026;30:195

Clinical example: the spectrogram as a mirror of systemic perfusion in septic shock (Fischer 2026)

Case report from Clínica Universidad de los Andes, Chile (Rev Chil Anest 2026;55:234–238). A 70-year-old man without comorbidity, septic shock with multi-organ failure after bowel perforation, APACHE II 29, SOFA 11, three vasoactive agents, high-volume haemofiltration. The unit uses frontal 4-channel pEEG with spectrogram (SedLine) routinely in all patients with continuous sedation or GCS below 8.

  • Early phase (skin hypoperfusion, high lactate): slow theta background (3.5–7 Hz), continuous diffuse delta and periods of suppression. Propofol was stopped because the theta background persisted, but deep sedation, theta and suppression episodes continued without sedation.
  • After haemodynamic improvement (adrenaline discontinued, milrinone started, lower vasopressor doses, better skin perfusion and organ function): alpha (8–13 Hz) and beta emerged, the suppression periods disappeared, and consciousness improved to SAS 3/RASS −2. Discharged home, Rankin 2 after six months.
  • The authors' interpretation: the systemic hypoperfusion coincided with burst suppression and slow waves, consistent with reduced cerebral perfusion even without known vascular disease; on improvement the fast waves returned. They refer to the CBF thresholds (fall in alpha and beta at 25–35 ml/100 g/min, increase in delta and theta below 17–18) and excluded seizures (standard EEG), structural injury (CT), hypothermia and metabolic causes.
  • Caveats: one patient, no direct measurement of cerebral blood flow, and sepsis encephalopathy in itself gives a slow EEG independent of perfusion, so the cause cannot be separated. The same phenomenon as Guay 2025 describes in the Perfusion tab.
Fischer et al. Rev Chil Anest 2026;55:234–238

Clinical example: unilateral suppression in an ECMO patient revealed a blood clot (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed. It is described from one screenshot of the spectrogram over about 17 minutes and information from the person who shared it. The screenshot is not reproduced in the app.

  • The patient: an ICU patient with COVID-19 on ECMO, sedated.
  • What the spectrogram showed: a clear difference between the hemispheres. In the upper panel activity was almost absent, interrupted only by short, scattered bursts, a picture resembling burst suppression. In the lower panel there was continuous activity with power in delta and even, low power up towards 30 Hz.
  • The course: according to the person who shared the case, there was a blood clot in the brain. It showed up nowhere other than in the EEG, and the patient was sent for intervention and recovered.
  • Why it is instructive: in a sedated patient the neurological examination is severely limited, and a stroke can be missed. Sedation acts on both hemispheres, so marked unilateral suppression argues against sedation alone being the explanation. This fits what van Putten and Hofmeijer and Sheorajpanday 2009 describe: ischaemia causes loss of activity and asymmetry. Nycz 2022 shows a similar asymmetry with carotid stenosis and low blood pressure.
  • What to do (the app's own synthesis): new or increasing asymmetry should first be checked for technical causes such as electrode contact and impedance. If the signal is good, it should prompt clinical assessment and imaging, not just adjustment of sedation.
  • Caveats: one case, described from one screenshot. It is not known which side and which vessel were affected, or which drugs and doses the patient received. A frontal monitor covers only a small part of the cortex and can miss infarcts elsewhere.
Shared clinical example van Putten and Hofmeijer 2016, Sheorajpanday 2009, Nycz 2022

Clinical example: comatose patient with only delta reacts when relatives visit (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed. It is described from two screenshots of the spectrogram and information from the person who shared it. The screenshots are not reproduced in the app.

  • The patient: a comatose ICU patient without sedation, with an EEG that for long periods showed only delta.
  • Without visitors: in one picture (about 20 minutes) the power in both hemispheres lay below about 4 Hz, with very little activity above. The picture was stable without changes.
  • With relatives present: in the other picture, power from theta up into beta, about 15–30 Hz, increased in both hemispheres in periods, while delta persisted.
  • What it may mean: a change in frequency or amplitude when the patient is stimulated is called EEG reactivity. Sutter and Kaplan 2012 write that reactivity distinguishes between coma states better than the pattern itself, and Miller's ch. 80 writes that preserved reactivity indicates a good outcome after anoxic brain injury. In three patients who eventually became independent after prolonged coma following cardiac arrest, reactivity returned after 3, 8 and 73 days (Forgacs 2020). This case shows that everyday stimuli, such as relatives' voices and touch, can produce a reaction visible on a frontal monitor.
  • What can be done (the app's own synthesis): test reactivity deliberately, with speech, touch and possibly a noxious stimulus, and note the time so the change can be found in the spectrogram. Repeat the test over days, since reactivity may return late.
  • Caveats: increased beta can also come from muscle activity (EMG), movement or other artefacts, so the raw EEG and the EMG indicator should be checked. Formal assessment of reactivity is done with standardised stimuli and a full EEG. One case, and the patient's outcome is not known.
Shared clinical example Sutter and Kaplan 2012, Miller's ch. 80, Forgacs 2020

Clinical example: alpha coma in an unconscious child turned out to be benzodiazepine poisoning (shared case)

One case from Norwegian clinical practice, shared with the author of this app. It is not published and not peer reviewed. It is described from one screenshot and information from the person who shared it. The screenshot is not reproduced in the app.

  • The patient: an unconscious 3-year-old child. At first it was unclear what had happened.
  • What the EEG showed: a strong, continuous band around 10–12 Hz in both hemispheres, together with delta, and little activity above about 20 Hz. The pattern was symmetrical and stable over about 20 minutes. The raw EEG showed regular, high-amplitude waves in the alpha range. The index was 34.
  • The explanation: it turned out to be a benzodiazepine overdose.
  • Link to the sources: Sutter and Kaplan 2012 describe alpha coma as alpha activity (8–13 Hz) in a patient who cannot be roused. In poisoning with barbiturates, benzodiazepines and anaesthetics among others, alpha is mostly frontal, reactivity is usually preserved and up to 90% recover. In hypoxic-ischaemic injury after cardiac arrest, alpha is more diffuse, reactivity is usually absent and the outcome is mostly poor. The same pattern can thus mean very different things depending on the cause.
  • Why it is instructive (the app's own synthesis): the pattern resembles alpha–delta under anaesthesia with propofol or sevoflurane. Benzodiazepines also act on the GABAA receptor (see the Drugs tab), and children generally have stronger alpha under GABAergic anaesthesia than adults (Lee 2017, Akeju 2015). In an unconscious patient of unknown cause, such a picture may therefore raise suspicion of a GABAergic drug. The diagnosis is nevertheless made clinically and with tests, not from the EEG alone.
  • Caveats: one case, described from one screenshot. Sutter and Kaplan mainly discuss adults. It is not known which benzodiazepine or dose, whether reactivity was tested, or how the child fared.
Shared clinical example Sutter and Kaplan 2012, Lee 2017, Akeju 2015

Fundamentals: what EEG is and how it is measured

This tab is for those without prior EEG knowledge: the signal, the frequency bands, the electrodes and montages, and what a TCI pump actually knows. Most of it builds on chapter 4 (“Basic Electroencephalography”, Greenblatt et al.) and chapter 5 in Lobo and Lamperti (2025). Further down are newer topics built on individual papers: nociception in the EEG (García 2021), aperiodic activity (Widmann 2025), hysteresis and emergence (Proekt and Kelz, Huang, Leroy, Connor) and TCI as a prediction. The other tabs assume this.

What EEG is

  • The signal: voltage differences in microvolts between electrodes on the scalp, created by summed postsynaptic potentials in large populations of cortical pyramidal cells lying in parallel. Action potentials contribute little. The signal from deep structures weakens with the square of the distance, and skull and skin attenuate the fast frequencies in particular.
  • History: Caton recorded spontaneous potentials from the animal brain in 1875. Hans Berger in Jena made single-channel recordings in humans, first in patients with skull defects, and published the first human EEG in 1929. Berger described alpha and beta waves, alpha blocking on visual stimulation, and the difference between adults and infants. Adrian and Matthews confirmed the findings in 1934 and gave Berger the credit.
  • What it shows and does not show: EEG describes cortical function in real time, not structure. It cannot say what the patient is thinking, only how the cortex is working. During anaesthesia it is the only routine measure of the target organ itself; all other monitors measure circulation, respiration or drug concentration.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 4

The frequency bands

  • Bands are a description, not a mechanism: the same frequency can have different origins. Frontal alpha under propofol (thalamocortical, see the Spectrogram tab) is not the same as posterior alpha in an awake person with eyes closed, even though both are 8–13 Hz.
  • Amplitude: the EEG signal is in the microvolt range and must be amplified to volt level before digitisation. Amplitude falls with age (Purdon 2015, Obert 2024) and increases with slow activity.
  • Gamma and EMG: gamma has low amplitude, is attenuated by skull and skin (Lobo and Lamperti ch. 4 write that 30–80 Hz is “typically filtered out by the skull and not visible on conventional surface EEG”) and overlaps in frequency with muscle activity. What looks like gamma on a frontal pEEG monitor in a patient without neuromuscular blockers is therefore often EMG from the forehead and eye muscles. In clinical neurophysiology it is precisely frontal EMG, blinking and eye movements that, together with low amplitude and fast activity, characterise an awake EEG; Schuller 2015 showed the flip side of this: in awake, paralysed volunteers the raw EEG looked awake “just without EMG and eye movements”, and BIS fell to 44–47 (see Schuller 2015 and Hight 2017 in the Spectrogram tab). The nuance: low gamma (25–40 Hz) under ketamine has been demonstrated with surface EEG in studies with good signal processing (Purdon 2015, Vlisides 2017), but in the clinic it cannot be distinguished from EMG without neuromuscular blockers.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 4 and 5

Electrodes, the 10–20 system and frontal monitors

  • The 10–20 system: electrodes are placed at 10% and 20% of the distances nasion–inion and between the preauricular points. The letters denote region (Fp frontopolar, F frontal, C central, T temporal, P parietal, O occipital), odd numbers left, even numbers right, z the midline. The standard set-up has 21 positions; the IFCN now recommends 25 with an inferior temporal row. Note that F7 and F8 actually lie over the anterior temporal lobe.
  • Impedance: modern equipment accepts up to 10 kΩ as long as the electrodes are balanced; below 100 Ω suggests a salt bridge or a fault. The skin is prepared to lower the impedance.
  • Amplifier and filters: the differential amplifier measures the difference between two inputs (active and reference) against ground. Anti-aliasing filter before digitisation (Nyquist: sampling frequency at least twice the highest frequency, recommended at least 256 Hz). For display, a low-pass filter (commonly 70 Hz), a high-pass filter (0.5–1 Hz) and a notch filter (50 Hz in Europe) are used. Too high a high-pass filter can hide precisely the slow activity that anaesthesia produces.
  • Montages: a bipolar montage shows the difference between two neighbouring electrodes, a referential montage shows each electrode against a common reference (ear, Cz or average). Lobo and Lamperti recommend using both, because they give complementary information; neither of them is “old-fashioned”. The Laplacian montage uses a weighted average of the neighbouring electrodes as a local reference.
  • Frontal anaesthesia monitors: all use only the anterior part of the 10–20 system. SedLine has a six-electrode strip with four channels over both sides (F7, Fp1, Fp2, F8, reference AFz, ground Fpz, as Mehler 2024 describes it). BIS is available with a unilateral sensor (four electrodes over one side of the forehead, the most widely used) and a bilateral sensor with electrodes over both sides; only the bilateral one can show asymmetry. Entropy (GE) is used at some Norwegian hospitals (Aasheim 2024), and Narcotrend also exists; both have their own frontal sensors with one or two channels. Common to all: sufficient for frontal alpha and slow activity under GABAergic agents, but not for lateralisation further back, seizure localisation or posterior alpha, and a unilateral sensor cannot tell the sides apart (see Nycz 2022 in the Perfusion tab). That is the background for the ICU literature (Rasulo 2023, Taccone 2026) distinguishing between questions that can be answered with a simplified montage and questions that require full 10–20.
Lobo and Lamperti 2025, ch. 4; Mehler 2024 (SedLine montage)

How EEG monitors are used in Norway (Aasheim 2024)

Cross-sectional survey with a web form sent to anaesthesia staff at all 54 Norwegian hospitals from autumn 2020 to June 2021 (Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2024;68:781–787), based on an Australian questionnaire (Ben-Menachem). 391 responded: 324 nurse anaesthetists and 67 anaesthetists, out of an estimated 1,800 and 1,500 in the country. More than half had over ten years of experience.

  • Access and use: 76% reported that a monitor was present in over 80% of operating rooms. 62% used it on more than half of their patients, 4% never. 49% had guidelines for use, 31% did not, 19% did not know. Used most often with neuromuscular blockade (68%), TIVA (43%) and obesity (29%); 22% “always when available”. 49% never used a monitor in children.
  • What is used: the index value in 99% of the anaesthetists and 98% of the nurses (BIS is the most widely used monitor, entropy exists at some hospitals). Raw EEG in 15% and 10%, spectrogram in 18% and 7%, suppression ratio in 18% and 9%, SEF95 in 1% and 3%. Heart rate (100%) and blood pressure (96%) were the dominant clinical signs, and 58% considered clinical signs more reliable than BIS.
  • Burst suppression: 27% reported that they could recognise the pattern (67% of the anaesthetists, 18% of the nurses, p < 0.0001), and 39% knew that it means too deep anaesthesia. At the same time, over 60% in both groups felt they had sufficient knowledge, and 86% wanted more.
  • Asymmetric dosing: 90% increased the dose at high index values, 55% reduced it at low values. Respondents were neutral to the statement that an index below 40 is associated with complications, and rated the monitor as more useful against awareness (76% agreed) than for reducing dose and emergence time. The authors interpret this as a stronger fear of awareness than of too deep anaesthesia.
  • Conclusion: widespread use, but the information beyond the index number (raw EEG, spectrogram, suppression) is little used, and the ability to recognise burst suppression is low. The authors call for training and more standardised guidelines. That is the background for this app.
  • Caveats: voluntary, anonymous web survey without a response rate that can be calculated reliably (about 18% of the nurses and 4% of the anaesthetists in the country), possible bias towards those who use the monitor a lot or are strongly opposed, no demographics (urban versus rural), self-reported knowledge. No conflicts of interest, no external funding. The discussion refers to BIS-guided anaesthesia reducing POCD at three months in older patients (ref. 19); see the Intensive care and Spectrogram tabs for the more divergent RCT evidence (ENGAGES, Evered 2021).
Aasheim, Rosseland, Leonardsen, Romundstad. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2024;68:781–787

Who gets the lowest BIS in Norwegian practice: age, sex and ASA (Aasheim 2026)

Observational cohort study from the four hospitals of Oslo University Hospital, 2017–2020 (Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2026;70:e70281). BIS values were extracted automatically from the electronic chart (MetaVision) and analysed with a linear mixed model with time, age, ASA and sex as covariates and patient as a random effect. Standard TIVA at the hospitals was Schnider TCI for propofol and Minto for remifentanil; 82% of BIS patients received TIVA.

  • Who was monitored: 97,733 patients received general anaesthesia, 26,650 (27%) had continuous BIS. BIS was used in 33% of TIVA patients versus 7% with volatile anaesthesia, and in only 21% of the 55,965 who received muscle relaxants. The proportion monitored fell with ASA class (ASA 1 TIVA 34%, ASA 4 TIVA 22%, ASA 4 volatile 4%). The typical BIS patient was ASA 1–2 on TIVA without relaxants, that is, not the patients at greatest risk of awareness and delirium. The authors call this unexpected and a patient-safety concern.
  • Who was deepest: in the adjusted model (table 3) men had BIS values 2.4 units higher than women (95% CI 2.3–2.8), each year of age lowered BIS by 0.05 (−0.055 to −0.045), and ASA 2, 3 and 4 were 0.2, 0.56 and 0.86 lower than ASA 1 respectively. Mean BIS rose with time into surgery (about 39 at the start), most clearly in ASA 1 (to nearly 48 after 300 min), whereas ASA 4 fell to around 30–35 (fig. 4). The differences are statistically secure because of the sample size but small in absolute terms; what is clinically interesting is the tails.
  • Burst-suppression level (BIS below 30): the proportion with a mean BIS below 30 for the whole procedure rose with ASA class, roughly 10% in ASA 1–2, 15% in ASA 3 and 22% in ASA 4 (fig. 5, read from the figure). At least 5 minutes below 30 occurred in about 26% of ASA 1 and 50% of ASA 4 (fig. 6). Mean BIS above 65 was rare (1–2%) and evenly distributed across sex and ASA. The authors cite Bruhn 2000: BIS below 30 corresponds to increasing suppression.
  • The authors' interpretation: lower BIS in the old and sick with standard Schnider TCI may mean that the model, or the way it is applied, is not sufficiently individualised for vulnerable patients; they cite Obert 2024 on slow induction (Spectrogram tab). Lower BIS in women may reflect clinicians perceiving female sex as a risk factor for awareness and dosing higher, or the Schnider model's fixed central volume (V1) not accounting for body composition, unlike Eleveld. They stress themselves that the associations should not be interpreted causally.
  • What is missing: only the BIS index was available, not raw EEG, suppression ratio or SEF, so artefacts and actual suppression could not be confirmed. No dosing data, no delirium data, BIS used selectively (not randomly), no pre-registration, and mean BIS hides within-procedure variation. The authors call for studies combining BIS with raw EEG, spectrogram and suppression measures, and measuring delirium in the frail.
  • The editorial comment in the journal points to what remains unresolved: whether deeper anaesthesia in the old and sick should be met with lower doses, or with better brain perfusion (see the Perfusion tab on autoregulation and alpha dropout).
  • Conflicts of interest: the authors declare no conflicts of interest and no funding. The study was approved by the data protection officer at OUS; the regional ethics committee judged that ethical approval was not required.
Aasheim, Rosseland, Ponzi, Kristiansen, Romundstad. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 2026;70:e70281

Artefacts and interpretation: where to find it

Eye movements, EMG, electrode movement, 50 Hz and ECG are described in the card “Artefacts and sources of error in EEG” in the Spectrogram tab. Reactivity and coma patterns are described in the Intensive care tab (Sutter and Kaplan 2012). Normal sleep phenomena (vertex waves, spindles, K-complexes) can resemble anaesthesia patterns; sleep spindles at 12–14 Hz during N2 have the same thalamocortical origin as frontal alpha under propofol, but not the same frequency or duration.

Aperiodic EEG activity (“1/f”): the background is signal, not noise

An EEG spectrum consists of two parts: periodic peaks (delta, theta, alpha, beta, which give the bands in the spectrogram) on top of an aperiodic background where power falls steadily with frequency according to a power law, P ∝ 1/fα. In a log-log plot the background is a straight line, and the exponent α is the slope: the steeper, the more the power is concentrated in the slow frequencies. This was long called “1/f noise”, but carries information.

  • The exponent follows hypnosis (Widmann 2025, BJA): frontal EEG in 62 awake subjects and 125 during maintenance with propofol, sevoflurane or desflurane, decomposed with the FOOOF algorithm. α was 1.61 awake versus 2.60 under anaesthesia (AUC 0.98). When the usual spectral parameters (beta ratio, SEF95, spectral entropy, alpha/delta ratio) were computed on the aperiodic model alone instead of the whole spectrum, the ability to separate awake from anaesthetised rose from AUC 0.71–0.95 to 0.98 for all four, on a par with permutation and approximate entropy. The authors' interpretation: the aperiodic part reflects the hypnotic component, while the periodic oscillations, especially alpha, disturb the indices and rather say something about the quality of the anaesthesia (nociception, frailty) than about the level of consciousness. Simulations (Gao 2017) link α to the balance between synaptic excitation and inhibition.
  • Age-independent markers of loss of consciousness (Leroy 2023): 9 young (18–30 years) and 14 older (over 70 years) subjects during manual propofol induction with 21 electrodes. Loss of consciousness produced an increased exponent and offset in both groups, the alpha peak shifted from about 10 to 11 Hz, and the adjusted alpha power above the background increased. The older subjects received half the propofol dose (1.8 versus 3.4 mg/kg), but 4 of 14 developed burst suppression versus 2 of 9 young. The young showed a “travelling” burst of power from gamma via beta to alpha around loss of consciousness (as in Purdon 2013), and in 8 of 9 young the exponent fell just before loss of consciousness, consistent with paradoxical excitation. When the background was subtracted, older and young looked far more alike: much of the age difference lies in the aperiodic part. Exploratory pilot without correction for multiple testing.
  • Why it matters in practice (Connor 2026, editorial): all of today's indices compute on the whole spectrum and treat all agents alike. Connor shows an example where a spectrogram does not reveal the agent, while the log-log slope does: β 2.70 in the example, close to what Dragovic 2025 found for sevoflurane (2.71) versus propofol (2.45). Brake 2024 furthermore showed that when the aperiodic part is subtracted, alpha and beta rise before loss of consciousness, while delta rises abruptly at loss of consciousness. The separation thus changes the interpretation of what happens when.
  • Links to the rest of the app: Kratzer 2020 and Purdon 2015 (BJA) describe lower power in older patients; Leroy suggests that much of that is the background, not the rhythms. Alpha as a “quality marker” fits with García 2021 (nociception), Gutiérrez 2019 (delirium) and Shao 2020 (low alpha and propensity for burst suppression). No commercial monitor displays the exponent today; this is research, not a clinical tool.
  • Caveats: Widmann is a signal-analytic study without control for doses or age, and the FOOOF settings (with or without a “knee” around 20 Hz) affect the numbers, so exponent values from different studies cannot be compared directly. Conflicts of interest: Kreuzer, García, Kratzer and Schneider hold patents on intraoperative EEG analysis, García is co-founder of Lantern Laboratories, Kreuzer has received funds from Masimo, Narcotrend, Medtronic and Fresenius for EEG teaching; Koch (Leroy 2023) holds patents sold to Medtronic. Connor reports none of relevance.
Widmann 2025, Leroy 2023, Connor 2026

Artefacts and pitfalls in processed EEG: the ANESTHESIA mnemonic (Pinheiro 2026)

Narrative review (Cureus 2026, PubMed to August 2025, selection at the authors' discretion). The point: the index alone cannot be trusted, and when it is unexpectedly high or low without an obvious reason, the sources of error should be gone through systematically. The authors group them in four.

  • Pharmacological: ketamine gives more beta/gamma and less delta and raises the index despite deeper anaesthesia. Dexmedetomidine and clonidine give spindles and slow waves and lower the index, also at moderate sedation. Nitrous oxide (an NMDA antagonist, like ketamine) changes the index little according to Pinheiro when given in usual adjunct doses on top of GABAergic anaesthesia, but Purdon 2015 (Part I) lists nitrous oxide with ketamine as the two agents that most often make clinicians doubt the index: both produce beta/gamma that tends to raise the index at clinically accepted doses, and on switching to above 70% nitrous oxide a transient, profound slow-delta pattern appears after 2–4 minutes before beta/gamma takes over. Abrupt withdrawal can lower the index paradoxically (“withdrawal-suppression”); rapid washout of isoflurane/sevoflurane can give a paradoxical low-voltage EEG with a falsely low index and burst suppression. Neuromuscular blockers lower the index by removing EMG, also in awake patients; sugammadex and neostigmine raise it, mostly via EMG, and sugammadex can produce an arousal effect under propofol. Opioids in analgesic doses change the index little, high doses can lower it. Neuraxial block lowers the index. Adrenaline, ephedrine, noradrenaline and isoprenaline (not phenylephrine) are reported to raise it; methylene blue and magnesium sulphate (RCT in obstetric patients under volatile anaesthesia) lower it.
  • Electromagnetic and mechanical: high impedance (temperature, humidity, poor skin preparation), pacemakers and other implants, diathermy, EMG tubes, facial nerve stimulators (even in standby, because of impedance testing), navigation equipment near the head, forced-air warming blankets near the head, endoscopic shavers, Doppler, pulsatile cardiopulmonary bypass and arterial pulsation (images 15 and 2 in the image quiz). SQI may remain high during such artefacts. ECG can dominate a low-voltage EEG.
  • Pathophysiological: age (the indices were built on adults; infants under 1 year and older patients deviate, see the Spectrogram tab), nociception (beta arousal, delta arousal, alpha dropout after García 2021), genetically low-voltage EEG in 5–10% of the population (check the baseline before induction), ischaemia, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, seizures and the post-ictal phase (a slow pattern that may persist after consciousness has returned), haemodynamics and positioning (forehead oedema in prolonged Trendelenburg), space-occupying lesions (side-to-side difference, a pseudomeningocele can mimic ictal activity), neurological disease (Alzheimer, vascular dementia, cerebral palsy give a lower index).
  • Model-dependent: different monitors, also from the same manufacturer, give different values at the same depth because of different algorithms and artefact filters; each new model has its learning curve.
  • ANESTHESIA (the mnemonic): Anaesthetic agents and other drugs (end-tidal/age-adjusted MAC, pump, TCI target, extravasation, backflow, occlusion); Neuromuscular blockade and reversal, neurological disease; Equipment (SQI, electrodes, sweat); Stimulus (nociception, nociception monitor, EEG patterns); Temperature, metabolism, tumour; Haemodynamics and positioning; Electromagnetic and mechanical interference; Seizure (pro- and anticonvulsants); Ischaemia and injury (NIRS if available); Age (infants, older patients). First: exclude dosing errors before other sources. Before induction: note the baseline index and DSA. If the artefact cannot be removed, it should at least be taken into account when the dose is adjusted.
  • Caveats: narrative review without systematic search or quality assessment; many claims rest on case reports. The authors stress that not every unexpected value is an artefact. One author reports speaker fees from MSD, unrelated to the work.
Pinheiro et al. Cureus 2026;18:e103656

What standards and consensus documents say about EEG monitoring

  • Norwegian standard for the safe practice of anaesthesia, 2024 revision (Leonardsen 2024): minimum monitoring in general anaesthesia is pulse oximetry, clinical assessment, ECG, blood pressure, oxygen alarm, capnography, disconnection alarm, multigas analysis with volatile agents and neuromuscular monitoring with non-depolarising blockers. “Monitoring of anaesthesia depth (e.g., BIS and EEG) must be individually considered.” The anaesthetic record must document monitoring equipment, with BIS given as an example. Adopted by the Norwegian Association of Anaesthesiologists and the Norwegian Association of Nurse Anaesthetists, in force from 1 March 2024; the authors declare no conflicts of interest.
  • Association of Anaesthetists 2021 (Klein 2021): processed EEG “should be used” when TIVA is given with a neuromuscular blocker, from before induction until full recovery from the block is confirmed, and “should be considered” with inhalational anaesthesia and in high-risk patients. The rationale is NAP5: most definite or probable awareness cases occurred with a neuromuscular blocker, and almost two-thirds before the start or after the end of surgery, where end-tidal gas monitoring does not help. With volatile anaesthesia an alarm at end-tidal below 0.7 age-adjusted MAC is recommended. And, quoted in substance: anaesthetists should not rely solely on the index value, but develop a basic understanding of the raw EEG, power spectrum, spectrogram and relative band powers. With manual charts pEEG should be recorded at least every 5 minutes. The first author reports educational grants/honoraria from, among others, Masimo (spelled “Massimo” in the article).
  • Definition and aims of anaesthesia, Delphi consensus (Berger-Estilita 2026): 23 experts, three rounds, 80% agreement as threshold, 49 aims in seven domains. Relevant aims: “a sufficient level of sedation/anaesthesia and avoid oversedation” (INT7), “protect cognitive functions and avoid postoperative delirium” (PRE5, DIS4, DIS5), “avoid long-term cognition disturbances” (LTO6), and “preserving or enhancing organ function, inclusive of brain and cognitive function” in the definition itself. The document does not mention EEG, but the aims are those EEG monitoring targets. Patient experiences (PREMs) were not included as aims. Several authors report honoraria or travel support from Medtronic and other suppliers.
  • Multinational Delphi consensus on TIVA (Uitenbosch 2022): 29 panellists, 79% European, 12 statements, strong consensus at ≥ 75%. Only four reached consensus: TIVA is useful in paediatric anaesthesia, reduces PONV, is better for the environment, and physiological effects (airway, haemodynamics) guide the choice. “The risk of awareness is an obstacle to TIVA” received only 20.6–21.5% agreement. Access to TCI pumps and pEEG was mentioned as a practical barrier, but the statement on practical obstacles did not reach consensus (34.4 → 64.3%).
